title: Ex-CFMEU boss admits to illegal tirade against AFL umpiring boss
text:
Former construction union boss John Setka is unapologetic for breaking workplace laws, with his barrister saying he did not "deliberately" wage a public campaign against an ex-building regulator and AFL umpiring chief.

Mr Setka, the former powerful Victorian secretary of the CFMEU, faces a fine of up to $18,730, but could be hit with a much heftier legal bill because the union has refused to indemnify his court costs.

The Federal Court on Friday heard Mr Setka admitted breaching the Fair Work Act by trying to coerce the AFL into sacking its head of umpiring Stephen McBurney in mid-2024.

Mr McBurney was the Australian Building and Construction Commissioner and participated in more than 50 court cases against the union between 2018 and 2023.

Mr Setka's barrister Margo Harris said her client should not receive a severe penalty.

She said he was now retired, in the middle of a divorce, and spent most of his time looking after his elderly mother.

"He doesn't express any remorse but he has made an admission that what he did was wrong," Ms Harris said.

Mr Setka was not in court for Friday's hearing.

Former union boss admits to breaching law

The development comes three days before the start of hearings in Victoria's Royal Commission into the state government's "Big Build" construction projects, which have been dogged by claims of widespread corruption and crime.

Mr Setka, who left the CFMEU weeks after his verbal attacks on Mr McBurney, is also facing separate criminal charges over alleged harassment of the union's administrators.

In the Fair Work case, Mr Setka was still union boss when he made social media posts and gave media interviews over a two-week period, threatening that the CFMEU would disrupt or delay AFL building projects if it did not get rid of Mr McBurney, the court heard.

"This is going to cost the AFL a lot of f**king money. I hope it's worth it," Mr Setka said.

"Projects without our full co-operation are going to be a f**king misery for them. They will regret the day they ever employed him."

John Setka left the CFMEU weeks after his verbal attacks on Stephen McBurney. (ABC News)

The Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO) prosecuted Mr Setka and the CFMEU, alleging the demands to sack Mr McBurney were made because of his lawful work as ABCC commissioner.

On Friday, barristers for Mr Setka and the CFMEU admitted to the breaches.

Ms Harris said there was no evidence Mr Setka "actively sought" media attention, even though he made statements to newspapers, and appeared in radio and television interviews where he said the AFL should sack Mr McBurney.

Ms Harris also said Mr Setka did not "deliberately" engage in a media campaign against Mr McBurney, prompting Federal Court judge John Snaden to clarify what she meant.

"When I say deliberate, there's a range of deliberateness. It's not a question of being pregnant or not pregnant," she replied.

"It comes in the stream of the interview. There's a question asked of him, he answers it."

However, FWO barrister Marc Felman said Mr Setka was not forced to give interviews.

"There can be no question that this is a media campaign," he said.

During one press conference, Mr Setka said of Mr McBurney: "He's a zealot. He hates unions. He hates workers in general."

He also put up a social media post depicting Mr McBurney in a mock poster containing the words: "(Not) Wanted Dead or Alive".

Penalty to be set for Setka and CFMEU despite claims of new regime

Mr Felman said Mr Setka's breaches of the Fair Work Act were "very, very serious".

He said Mr Setka wasn't the first person to call for the sacking of an AFL umpire, but it became illegal because the demands were connected to Mr McBurney's lawful work in an old job.

Mr McBurney, who has umpired four grand finals, was backed by the AFL at the time and remains the league's head of officiating.

Stephen McBurney adjudicated 401 AFL games and is still employed as the league's head of officiating. (AFLUA Hall of Fame)

The CFMEU, which has since been taken over by administrators, could be fined up to $93,900.

Barrister Andrew White, for the CFMEU, called for the penalty to be moderated because the union's new regime no longer saw breaking the law as "the cost of doing business".

He said the cultural shift had occurred following hundreds of Setka-era officials being removed or leaving their jobs.

"A new culture of lawful but robust unionism is taking hold," he said.

Justice Snaden will set the penalty for Mr Setka and the CFMEU at a later date.

title: Paraguay's president tangled up in Ueno banking crisis
text:
It only took two days for Paraguayan president to resign after a banking crisis blocked nearly half of the small South American country's population from accessing their money.

The central bank's takeover of Ueno Bank plunged the country into a political crisis, sparking protests and a move to unanimously launch impeachment proceedings against President Santiago Peña in Congress.

The US-allied leader beat them to the punch by resigning on X minutes beforehand.

How did Paraguay get here?

It all came crashing down on Monday when regulators investigating Ueno Bank uncovered alleged excessive lending to companies linked to its controlling shareholder, Grupo Vázquez, and expenses wrongly counted as assets.

By Tuesday, the central bank seized control of the digital lender due to a severe capital shortfall, and authorities issued arrest warrants for eight of Ueno's top executives.

Executives of Ueno Bank arrive in custody at the anti-corruption prosecutor's office in Asuncion, Paraguay. ( AP Photo/Jorge Saenz)

The bank's president Miguel Vazquez turned himself into police and central bank president Carlos Carvallo stepped down at Mr Pena's request.

Mr Carvallo, who was president of Ueno's predecessor, was appointed the top job at the central bank — the agency charged with supervising Ueno — by Mr Peña.

As recently as last month, Mr Peña defended Ueno which reported holding roughly $800 million in public deposits, including money from the state pension and health fund and the operators of Paraguay's giant hydro-electric dams.

Mr Peña, a former International Monetary Fund economist, also owned shares in the group that controlled the digital lender until last year.

Peña scrambles to contain the situation

On Wednesday Mr Peña enacted a law to return most deposits within five days.

Thirty-five lawmakers meanwhile filed a motion to impeach him.

By Thursday, Mr Pena's own Colorado Party turned against him, with party leader Horacio Cartes announcing that he backed impeachment.

The Chamber of Deputies opened a session to debate the motion, but no sooner had it started than Mr Peña posted a video on X announcing his resignation.

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña signs his resignation letter at the government residence in Asunción, Paraguay. (AP Photo/Laura Fioravanti)

"I want to apologise to the people if at any point I failed. It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," he said.

Minutes later, the 78 deputies present unanimously approved the impeachment motion against Mr Peña.

Both houses have since declined to accept his offer to resign, pressing forward with a trial that could result in the president's removal from office.

Opposition senators said allowing him to resign would preserve his eligibility to become a senator for life and grant him with legal protections preventing his prosecution.

If the presidency remains vacant, Vice President Pedro Alliana will complete the term until 2028.

Peña faces criminal investigation

Paraguay's Attorney General Emiliano Rolón Fernández has ordered three criminal investigations into the Ueno Bank crisis, including allegations involving Mr Peña and other current and former government officials.

The investigations will examine authorities' oversight of the bank, their handling of its failure and the placement of public funds in the lender.

Mr Peña said he would cooperate with investigators.

"Whatever the outcome of this process, I will act with responsibility and respect for the Constitution," he said on X.

What is Ueno?

Ueno Bank, exploded from an obscure local fintech company into a mid-sized Paraguayan bank in less than five years, claiming more than 60 per cent of Paraguay's adults as customers.

Ueno Bank says it has over 3 million customers in a country of 6.4 million people and manages millions of dollars in pensions and other state funds.

Soon after winning its banking licence in 2023, Ueno seemed to be everywhere.

The headquarters of Ueno Bank in Asuncion, Paraguay. (AP: Jorge Saenz)

The digital lender, a rebranded version of a decades-old finance company, lured customers with generous cash-back offers on groceries as it grew to more than 70 locations, sponsored Paraguay's national soccer team and plastered its name on the country's main stadium.

The bank's rapid expansion made it one of Paraguay's most visible financial success stories.

Its collapse has triggered days of protesting in the country.

"Santiago Peña and the Colorado Party have stolen all our savings," said Luis Pineda, one of the protesters marching to Congress.

Police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse the crowds who shouted "give us our money back".

Wires

title: 'Not a waste of money': Authority to be dissolved after years of issues
text:
The troubled regional waste authority responsible for the collapse of Western Australia's first food organics and garden organics (FOGO) system is being dissolved.

The Bunbury Harvey Regional Council (BHRC) was in charge of operating two waste facilities, including the FOGO processing facility which began in 2013.

Banksia Road Organics Processing Facility near Dardanup, 180 kilometres south of Perth, closed indefinitely in late 2024 due to high levels of contamination in breach of composting standards.

Ratepayers were left with a $2 million bill to remove tonnes of FOGO waste at BHRC's organic processing facility in Dardanup. (ABC South West: Ella Lonergan)

The closure resulted in the South West's green-bin waste being sent straight to landfill.

City of Bunbury and Shire of Harvey have now made an in-principle agreement to disband the joint waste management authority.

Some of the South West councils have decided to continue to send their FOGO to landfill, while others have taken up a state government subsidy to have the waste trucked to the Perth processing facility.

Mayor denies failure

In a joint statement, both councils said they had agreed BHRC's governance model was no longer financially, operationally or environmentally sustainable.

Bunbury Mayor Jaysen Miguel said the dissolution did not amount to a failure.

"I wouldn't call this a failure. There has been a lot of work over this place for a long time," he said.

The future for the staff and management of the waste authority is yet to be decided.

BHRC's Banksia Rd organics processing facility stopped accepting FOGO in late 2024 due to high rates of contamination. (ABC South West: Bridget McArthur)

Both councils will now create a draft transition plan which is expected to be finalised early next year.

The cost of compliance

Financial reports show South West ratepayers have poured $14.7 million into BHRC's operations since 2022, when regulatory scrutiny began mounting over its operations.

In 2022, the Department of Water and Environmental Regulation (DWER) shut down on-site landfilling at BHRC's other waste facility, the Stanley Road Waste Management Facility near Australind.

The tip at Stanley Road was turned into a transfer station after issues with overflowing landfill and leaking contaminants. (ABC South West: Georgia Loney)

The regulator raised concerns about the "unacceptable" risk to human and environmental health from full and unlined landfill cells leaching contaminants into the surrounding area.

Both councils paid a combined $7.7 million in 2022/23 towards operating costs and remediation at Stanley Road tip to stop further contamination.

The Stanley Road tip has since operated as a household waste transfer and drop-off station.

The waste authority again got into trouble in 2023 for storing 15,000 used mattresses, creating an "extreme fire risk".

In November 2025, both councils agreed to contribute $2 million to remove a 20,000-tonne stockpile of contaminated FOGO waste at the Banksia Road site.

'Not a waste of money'

BHRC chairperson Wendy Dickinson defended the millions of dollars spent on remediation.

"The funding that has been put in by the member councils has been used to meet compliance issues, which we have been in the process of addressing and continuing to do," she said.

" So that has not been a waste of money. "

Ms Dickinson said the dissolution was simply recognition of changing legislation, compliance requirements and infrastructure needs since the authority was established in 1990.

Former Bunbury councillor and deputy mayor Brendan Kelly said the waste authority had been a "black hole" for ratepayer money.

The regulator intervened in 2023 when BHRC stockpiled thousands of old mattresses and created an "extreme fire risk". (Supplied: Bunbury Harvey Regional Council)

"Both of those councils have been bleeding money over the last decade on trying to manage their waste, and they're not getting anywhere," he said.

"Harvey and Bunbury need to get themselves together and do not leave the room until they have a well-thought-out plan," he said.

"There's no point in just saying, 'too hard'. That's not the solution."

The former councillor said the problems at BHRC were symptomatic of a much wider failure to plan for the South West's waste-management needs.

"The BHRC and Stanley Road are not the disease, it's the symptom," he said.

"Successive state governments have kicked the can down the road when it comes to waste management in the South West."

Brendan Kelly says the two councils need to work harder for a waste solution. (ABC South WEst WA: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet)

He said the region's councils needed to work alongside the state government to develop a centralised, long-term waste-management strategy.

The WA local government minister has been contacted for comment.

title: Baseballer loses sight in one eye in 'horrific freak accident'
text:
Adelaide's baseball community is rallying around a "tough cookie" player who lost sight in one eye after a "horrific freak accident" during a weekend game.

Veteran member of the Adelaide Angels Baseball Club, Tyler Forney, was struck in the eye by a foul ball off his own bat, during a double-header against Woodville on Saturday.

Close friend and long-time teammate Chris Congdon said Mr Forney was in the batter's box during the second game when the incident happened.

"His ball ricocheted off his bat and basically collected his right eye," Mr Congdon said.

"[It] resulted in him getting taken off to hospital by ambulance in a bad way and having significant eye surgery that evening.

"However, he's permanently lost vision in his right eye as a result of that.

"Anyone I've spoken to around the club that was there was just really mortified by the accident … it's a really horrific freak accident."

Mr Congdon said Mr Forney was an integral member of the club since joining back in 2016, after moving from Arizona in the United States.

He said Mr Forney had a gifted athletic ability which he had honed while playing college baseball.

"He's a really really tough cookie, Ty — I'm sure he played through a broken hand for parts of last season," Mr Congdon said.

"He was a walking highlight reel, he would make plays at shortstop that just no one else could make.

"He just stuck with us and [he's] a massive reason why the last five years we've had huge success."

'So grateful' for support

A GoFundMe page has since raised more than $16,200 by Friday afternoon to cover Mr Forney's medical fees.

"He [Mr Forney] did not realise how much of an impact that he has had on people — not only in our club, but the wider baseball community," Mr Congdon said.

" He's a very humble person, but this has really, really taken him taken by surprise and he's just so grateful. "

Mr Congdon said Mr Forney was being supported by his partner, two children and three stepchildren as he recovers.

He said while Mr Forney's playing career may have come to an end, the club is already talking about ways to transition him to a coaching role.

"He's the sort of person that is quite private and reserved, but when he speaks and he does, everybody listens, so I think he wouldn't have thought about coaching," he said.

"He had so much left to do as a player and still so valuable as a player."

title: Seasonal produce to make the most of this November
text:
"I'm definitely excited for more chopped salads with lots of different colours," Phoebe Thorburn says.

Thorburn, a writer and cook in Naarm/Melbourne, says spring produce "is easier to eat closer to its natural form", which also helps with the cooking "mental load".

Josh Ball, co-founder of home delivery grocer Farmers Pick, says shopping seasonally tends to leave you with the freshest, tastiest and cheapest produce.

Josh Ball says asparagus has had a plentiful season that will begin to wrap up in the next few weeks. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

"Cost of living is a massive consideration and following the seasons is the best way to get the best price," he says.

There's new produce, such as mangoes and cherries, to be excited about and year-round staples too.

While brassicas grow all year, "the more sunshine they get, the faster they grow" and November can see prices drop, Ball says.

What can you look for?

Vegetables:

Broccoli

Cauliflower

Cabbage

Asparagus

Broad beans

Corn

Zucchini

Avocado

Garden peas

Snow peas

Fresh garlic

Fruit:

Mangoes

Strawberries

Cherries

Other stone fruit, such as nectarines, peaches and apricots, are expected later this month

Brassicas (those old favourites)

Spring weather often brings on a good supply of brassicas, particularly broccoli, cauliflower and cabbage, Ball says.

"If there's some sunny days in a row, they come on really fast," he says, and you can suddenly have a flush of affordable and versatile cauliflowers.

And if you're shopping at smaller or independent grocers, prices can change quickly, he says.

Enjoy asparagus and broad beans (while you can)

Hamish Franklin, the buyer at Georgie's Harvest in South Melbourne Market, says white and green asparagus will be available for the next few weeks.

Four spring asparagus recipes From one-pot pasta to a crunchy green salad, these easy recipes will put spring asparagus on your weeknight menu.

"When you're buying regular asparagus, you want to find the bigger size [spears], which have got a deeper, richer flavour," he says.

But, Thorburn gets "really excited about the baby asparagus".

"I've been wanting to make, like, a warm, tangy, vinaigrette potato salad with asparagus," they say.

Ball says: "If you like asparagus, you've probably got a few more weeks to really enjoy it and then it'll probably start disappearing."

Broad beans have a "relatively short season" and will be "winding up as well", he says.

Alan Li, from Fruits on Coventry in South Melbourne Market, expects broad beans to be available until the end of the month.

Broad beans are also known as fava beans, particularly once dried. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

Corn and zucchini

While corn is reasonably priced currently, Li says the price will drop as the volume increases.

The zucchini supply will increase in Australia's south in the next few weeks too, he says.

Zucchini and corn are also among Thorburn's warmer weather favourites, and they recommend charring corn cobs on a griddle pan and using the kernels in salads and salsas or sautéing thinly sliced zucchini "coins" in olive oil and butter as a side.

"Sometimes adding peas in, sometimes asparagus, [and] seasoning it."

Phoebe Thorburn says they have "gone a bit hard" on turning zucchini into fritters and slice in the past. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

Mangoes

Making mango lassis and dicing mango for salads is great, but like a lot of us, Thorburn is most excited for just eating mangoes out in the sun.

Josh Ball says mango is "definitely a superstar fruit coming into summer". (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

The first mangoes came from the Northern Territory in early spring. However, Ball says supplies are now beginning to come from Queensland.

"People can expect to see mangoes coming into that sort of affordable, bingeable territory over the next couple of weeks, which is pretty exciting," Ball says.

Li says the Kensington prides are "Australia's best-eating mangoes" and he recommends the firmer flesh of the R2E2 variety for salads.

Berries, cherries and other stone fruit

Li says a lot of interesting fruit is coming into season this month.

This includes Victorian strawberries, which are becoming less expensive, he says, as well as other berry varieties, such as raspberries, blackberries and mulberries.

Josh Ball says a lot of cherries are rejected for aesthetic reasons. (ABC News: Anna Chisholm)

Ball is already stocking cherries, which can be "volatile" to grow.

"If there's any poorly timed rain, or hail in particular, the whole crop can be destroyed pretty easily," he says.

You might not have seen other stone fruit on the shelves yet, but Ball says it's on the way, pointing to the Goulburn Valley and northern Victorian growing regions.

So expect nectarines, peaches and apricots later in November.

"And then obviously through summer they're everywhere and they can get pretty cheap if it's a good season," Ball says.

title: Man sues former AFL players Dion Prestia and Steven May
text:
A man is suing former AFL players Dion Prestia and Steven May over an alleged brawl on Victoria's Mornington Peninsula.

The two players were previously charged over an alleged streetside altercation with another group in the coastal town of Sorrento on Boxing Day in 2024, but the charges were dropped in May 2026.

Mr Prestia, a former Richmond premiership player, had been charged with recklessly causing serious injury and affray, while Mr May, an ex-Demons player who retired this year, was charged with affray.

The incident left two men in hospital with non-life-threatening injuries.

Previously, both Mr Prestia and Mr May strenuously denied their involvement in the alleged incident.

A personal injury claim is now underway in the Supreme Court over the alleged assault.

It is understood medical costs are among the damages being sought by a single plaintiff, who claims he was assaulted.

His name has been restricted by the court.

Court documents containing the exact details of the claim are yet to be released.

At a directions hearing in the Supreme Court on Friday, lawyers confirmed two more defendants were being added to the civil case alongside Mr May and Mr Prestia.

Their criminal matters remain before the court which means civil action is unlikely to commence before their cases are finalised.

Mr Prestia played 254 games for Richmond and Gold Coast and is a three-time premiership player.

It was recently announced he would join Hawthorn's coaching line-up for the 2027 season as an AFL development coach.

Mr May played 251 AFL games for Melbourne and Gold Coast and was a member of the Demons' 2021 premiership-winning squad.

He retired suddenly on the eve of the 2026 season.

Mr Prestia's employer and Mr May have been contacted for comment.

title: Qantas flags fare increases and flight cuts as fuel prices surge
text:
The Middle East war continues to weigh on Qantas, which says higher airfares and flight cuts are on the horizon despite strong domestic and international demand.

High jet-fuel costs driven by the conflict saw hundreds of millions shaved off the airline's last annual profit.

"The Qantas Group continues to experience trading conditions in line with the outlook provided at its [financial year 2026] results in August, despite elevated fuel prices," Qantas said in a market update released on Friday morning.

"The Group has and will continue to adjust fares and capacity in response to higher fuel costs."

The statement, released ahead of the carrier's annual general meeting, said domestic flights for Qantas and Jetstar would be cut by a total of four per cent in 2027.

Qantas said it expected fuel costs of $3.8 billion for the first half of the new financial year, and said it had extended hedging for about 85 per cent of its annual bill, predominantly in Brent crude oil.

Hedging is a strategy that is typically used to reduce or offset the risk of financial loss due to unpredictable market movements.

Brent crude oil now sits above $US100 a barrel, up from about $US60 before the US attacked Iran in February.

"Fuel prices are expected to remain elevated through financial year 2027," Qantas said.

The announcement on flight cuts and price rises comes despite strong demand for international and domestic travel, which Qantas said was "supported by customers redirecting travel away from the Middle East".

Corporate and government travel remained stable and was being closely monitored, it said.

The group also cut domestic flight capacity and raised fares in April, citing fuel costs.

In August, the airline reported a 2025/26 net profit of $1.3 billion, down nearly 20 per cent on the previous year.

Its underlying pre-tax profit also fell by nearly 14 per cent to $2.1 billion, despite a 7 per cent rise in revenue to $25.5 billion.

The carrier has also cancelled a planned $150 million share buyback.

Meanwhile, Qantas is still forecasting total revenue per available seat kilometre (TRASK) — a core metric used by the airline industry to measure unit revenue — to rise by up to 10 per cent in the first half of 2026/27 mostly driven by international travel.

The airline's capital expenditure is now expected to be at the lower end of the previously guided range of $4.3 billion to $4.6 billion.

Qantas predicts its new non-stop Project Sunrise flights from Australia to Europe and North America will earn $400 million a year once all the planes are flying by 2031.

ABC/AAP

title: Christmas display burns down in Canberra shopping centre
text:
A Christmas display at a shopping centre in Canberra's north has been cordoned off after a Christmas tree caught fire early this morning.

Just before 5am, emergency services were alerted to a blazing tree as part of the display at Westfield Belconnen.

The cause of the fire has yet to be determined. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

Christmas decorations, including elves, were damaged in the fire, but the large Christmas tree next to the display was untouched by the blaze.

ACT Fire and Rescue crews said they cut down a tree in the display and extinguished the fire at the scene.

Emergency services said the fire was not suspicious. (ABC News: Monte Bovill)

There was no damage to the surrounding areas in the shopping centre.

Authorities have not confirmed the cause of the fire, but did say it was not suspicious.

A Westfield Belconnen spokesperson said, "The incident was promptly attended to by authorities, with the support of our team".

"Santa's arrival at Westfield Belconnen tomorrow will continue as planned.

"The Santa Set will be temporarily unavailable during this time.

"Some customers' Santa Photography bookings will be rescheduled, and those impacted will be contacted directly by our team."

title: Coalition promises compensation access for firefighters who get cancer
text:
Firefighters who develop cancer as a result of their service will have better access to compensation if the Coalition wins the state election later this month.

Victorian Opposition Leader Jess Wilson has promised to expand presumptive rights legislation for firefighters, bringing it in line with other states.

Victorian firefighters are covered by presumptive rights legislation which ensures they are entitled to compensation if diagnosed with certain types of cancer.

The law only applies to firefighters who developed one of a list of cancers, having worked in an approved position.

Former Country Fire Authority (CFA) technical field officer Simon Lund spent his final days campaigning to have the law changed before he died of oesophageal cancer. He was unable to access the legislation due to not holding an approved job title.

Simon Lund (middle) was not covered under the presumptive rights legislation. (Supplied: Tracie Lund)

Ms Wilson said not enough cancers were covered in Victoria, compared to other states, including Queensland.

She said a Liberal government would expand the program to cover thyroid and lung cancer.

"To ensure that our firefighters in the FRV but also CFA, our volunteers, have access to that through WorkSafe," Ms Wilson said.

Victoria's election is nearly here — it's time to have Your Say Before Victorians head to the polls on November 28, we want to hear about what matters to you most.

It is unclear whether the Coalition's plan would also expand the approved job titles applicable under the scheme.

A Labor spokesperson did not state whether they would match the Coalition promise, instead labelling the pledge "dodgy costings from Jess Wilson".

Promises continue

The Coalition has also promised $160 million over four years to modernise Fire Rescue Victoria's aging fleet, with $40 million allocated annually to replace vehicles.

The United Firefighters Union estimates 138 fire trucks, or 65 per cent of FRV's vehicles, are past the end of their service life.

The Coalition has also promised a review of firefighter handsets and fireground communications, and a helmet replacement program.

A Labor spokesperson questioned the Coalition's ability to deliver on the election promise.

"You simply cannot deliver all this for $160 million," the spokesperson said.

"Jess Wilson’s $40 billion cuts plan will devastate our emergency services and put Victorians at risk.

"Labor has a fully costed plan to deliver firefighters the trucks they need, without cutting."

Presumptive rights legislation aims to ease the burden of compensation cases for firefighters diagnosed with cancer. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)

Opposition spokesperson for Fire Rescue Victoria, Nick McGown, said modern firefighting equipment was crucial.

"Our firefighters put their lives on the line to protect us, and we owe it to them and every Victorian family to ensure they have the vehicles, equipment and resources needed to respond quickly, safely and effectively when disaster strikes," he said.

Firefighters welcome announcement

Justin Seddon is the captain of the Nar Nar Goon Fire Brigade, in Victoria's south-east, whose brigade has recorded 22 cancer cases among long-serving members, including three deaths.

Almost half of the firefighters are not eligible for compensation under state government compensation schemes.

Justin Seddon says expanding presumptive rights legislation is good news for firefighters. (ABC News: Lily Kristanto)

In Victoria, presumptive protections only apply to certain cancers, but exclude cancers such as thyroid and lung cancer.

Mr Seddon said the Liberal promise would be well received.

"This is something that volunteer firefighters have been fighting for for a long time, to bring the legislation in line with other states," he said.

"What this means is that we've got protection now. It means that our families, if we do become sick, will be protected and the legislation is there to support us going forward."

title: Probe widens after steering failure on Spirit of Tasmania ferry
text:
The transport safety watchdog has expanded its probe into steering issues on the new Spirit of Tasmania ferries after the primary system "failed" on one of the ships on Thursday.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) was already investigating an incident involving Spirit V during a trial voyage on October 24.

During that incident, steering problems involving the autopilot briefly caused the ship to move outside the charted shipping channel limits off Geelong.

'Steering issue' cause delay on new Spirit ferry Days after its maiden voyage, one of the new Spirits has been escorted by a tugboat to Geelong.

Yesterday, Spirit IV suffered its own steering issue that resulted in a tugboat escorting the vessel to Geelong as a precaution.

At a Public Accounts Committee hearing today, TT-Line's chief executive Chris Carbone said the new ships had two separate steering systems as a redundancy.

"Those systems are independent of each other and, in fact, they're made by different manufacturers and that's part of the whole safety systems on board the ship," Mr Carbone said.

"So [in] yesterday's incident, the primary system failed.

" We moved to the backup system and because we had no further backup, that's why the tug was called. "

TT-Line chairman Ken Kanofski apologised to passengers for the four-hour delay caused by the issue, but said safety took precedence over scheduling.

"Yesterday we had an operational issue," Mr Kanofski told the committee.

"All of the backup systems and procedures kicked into place.

"All of the protocols were followed.

" The captain was always in control of the ship and at all times passengers and crew were safe. "

Spirit of Tasmania IV arrived in Geelong four hours behind schedule. (ABC News: Harrison Tippet)

Mr Carbone said it was not yet known if the steering issues on both vessels involved the same root cause.

He said TT-Line had appointed an independent investigator to assess both incidents.

"I want to assure everyone that these new ships are safe and they also have full redundancy across all the operating systems on the ship," he said.

Spirit IV resumed service overnight.

The transport safety watchdog has broadened its investigation into steering issues on the new Spirit of Tasmania ferries. (ABC News: Maren Preuss)

'Highest investigation priority': ATSB

The ATSB said yesterday's incident would now be included in a wider probe of the October 24 incident.

"The expanded investigation will involve the download of both ships' vessel data recorders for the relevant voyages, examining the ships' equipment, interviewing involved crew and other relevant personnel, and analysing records and documentation," the ATSB said.

" This broadened investigation is in line with the ATSB's highest investigation priority in the marine transport mode being occurrences involving Australian-flagged passenger vessels. "

Switch from auto control to manual failed, ATSB says

In a summary posted on its website on Friday, the ATSB also provided further details about what happened during the November 5 incident involving Spirit IV.

"When steering control was changed from the autopilot to manual mode (follow-up), the steering wheel did not respond to helm commands," it said.

"Control was then changed to emergency non-follow-up to embark the pilot while the ship's engineers attempted to correct the fault.

"Once the pilot was on board, the ship aborted entry to Port Phillip Bay to further investigate the issue.

"Further attempts to transfer steering to manual mode were unsuccessful.

" Subsequently, steering control was transferred to the bridge wing and central steering levers from where the ship was then steered. "

The ATSB is also investigating a third incident in which the master of Spirit I was forced to abort entry into Port Phillip Bay due to a position error on the ship's electronic chart display on October 15.

Investigation into Spirit of Tasmania navigational issue The investigation intends to uncover whether a technical fault or human error contributed to the issue.

Spirit I and Spirit II have since been retired from service as part of TT-Line's delayed and over-budget ferry replacement program.

The two older ships are berthed in Victoria while TT-Line tries to secure buyers for each vessel.

"We are in very advanced discussions," Mr Kanofski told the committee.

"Further advanced on one than the other."

The committee was told it was hoped one of the ships would be sold by the end of December and the other by mid next year.

title: Injured MP Helen Haines's condition improved to 'stable'
text:
Federal MP Helen Haines is in a stable condition in hospital, more than two weeks after she was critically injured when she was struck by a car outside her electorate office in Victoria's north-east.

Ms Haines was flown to hospital in Melbourne after the alleged attack in Wangaratta on October 19.

The 65-year-old was unloading the boot of her car after attending an event in Mansfield when she was struck and pinned between two vehicles.

As a result of the independent MP's injuries, both of her legs were amputated in hospital.

Floral tributes grew at Helen Haines' Wangaratta office in the days after she was allegedly attacked. (ABC News: Annie Brown )

The Alfred Hospital said in a statement this afternoon that Ms Haines's condition was now "stable".

She had been in a "serious but stable" condition since October 23, when she was downgraded by her medical team from a critical condition.

The hospital said Ms Haines' family would not be making any statements to the media.

Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the federal offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official over the incident.

He made a brief appearance in court in the days after the alleged attack and was remanded in custody.

The court heard he had some mental health concerns, and suffered from a rare neurological condition.

Mr Nugent is due to appear again in court in February.

Tributes poured in for the MP in the days after the alleged attack, with both locals and her colleagues in Canberra speaking of her kindness and passion for rural communities.

A sea of flowers were left outside the electoral office in Wangaratta, and hundreds of thousands of dollars were donated to charity Save the Children at the request of her family.

Ms Haines's husband Phil said his partner of 40 years was a fighter, with a "huge heart" and sharp intellect.

The incident sparked national debate about the direction of political discourse in Australia and the abuse directed at politicians.

A number of MPs have since detailed the toll of abuse they have experienced in their electorates, including ahead of the Victorian state election on November 28.

Speaking alongside Ms Haines's husband Phil in the days after the incident, Governor-General Sam Mostyn urged Australians to "disagree well", and that society needed to exercise their muscle of decency.

Nothing sours a voter quite like soaring living costs and a war nobody asked for. Donald Trump found that out the hard way this week as Democrats swept the midterms, taking both the House and the Senate. Even his own Vice President, JD Vance, pinned the loss on the war in Iran, which has dragged on since February and sent petrol and power bills through the roof. Oil got the memo first, with Brent sliding almost 9 per cent in a day to just under US$95 a barrel as traders bet a Democrat-run Congress will push for peace in the Middle East. Wall Street, meanwhile, partied for about 24 hours before Thursday came and the penny dropped. This week’s Bulls N’ Bears ASX Runner of the Week is… BPM Minerals. The extremely AI-heavy Wall Street has been running on the AI trade almost single-handedly for the last four months. AI needs data centres, data centres need electricity and voters furious about their electricity bills have just handed power to a party swearing to slow the whole build-out.

Advertisement

The Nasdaq fell a massive 5.5 per cent Thursday, with the S&P 500 shedding 4.4 per cent, its worst day since Trump’s tariff tantrum back in April. That left the Nasdaq in correction territory and US$2 trillion lighter. Copper, the metal that wires all those data centres together, copped it too. Then came the so-called Magnificent Seven, which could no longer hold the NASDAQ on its shoulders, shedding more than US$1 trillion in market value in a single session. Nvidia, the poster child of the AI boom, sank more than 9 per cent, with Tesla diving almost 11 per cent. Back home, the cost of living wasn’t getting any government reprieve at all. Same government, same rate outcome. The RBA turned up on Melbourne Cup Day and said its tired old ‘please stop spending’ line, but this time, not to the consumer. With the rate rise Aussies feared arriving, cash rates were lifted to 4.85 per cent, hitting an 18-year high.

Advertisement

Governor Michele Bullock was blunt that oil isn’t the reason. The problem is domestic demand outrunning supply – cough government spending. Awkward, then, for Treasurer Dr Jim Chalmers and Albo, who spent the week pointing the finger at oil. Fresh off 18 holes at the newly $6 million revamped Marrickville Golf Club, where, after previously denying he ever played golf, Albo defended his grant - worth 76 times all Australian golf grants combined this year - as a sewage fix, before admitting he “was not correct”. Hard to see how crude prices did that. Now the PM has suddenly discovered the need for “hard decisions” on government spending. Apparently, it only took a trillion dollars in debt for the penny to drop. After a budget that landed a body blow to industry and small business, Dr Jim’s much-promised cost-of-living relief is looking increasingly like another round of higher mortgage repayments. And just when you thought tech couldn’t look more toppy, Binance, the world’s biggest crypto exchange, lost a record US$6.3 billion to the North Koreans last Friday, following a fake job interview and a tampered AI tool to one of its employees. It seems Rocket Man’s boys have been having a very good week. Unconfirmed hackers have also been cooking the fridges and freezers of European supermarkets, with one Swedish store hitting 50 degrees Celsius on overdrive. UK cyber officials say the French units were plugged straight into the internet with default passwords. Which raises the question: why is a fridge connected to hackable infrastructure at all? Apparently so head office can check the temperature from afar, which is handy right up until someone else wants to turn the dial.

Advertisement

Amid all the week’s red, there was one shiny yellow lining. Gold jumped more than three per cent on the midterms, its biggest one-day gain since August, to reclaim US$4,000 an ounce and sit roughly six per cent higher on the week. Our Runner of the Week is back on old faithful too, with a geologist’s favourite words, “greenfields discovery”, coming out of WA’s Eastern Goldfields. There’s something reassuring about a hole in the ground: nobody has found a way to hack one yet. “First-ever drilling on massive target, hitting high-grade gold”. Nothing gets the imagination firing quite like that headline. BPM Minerals is drilling its Forelands project, 150km east of Kalgoorlie, to test its Bonnie & Clyde prospect, an untested 6km-long anomaly exhibiting the footprint of a major gold deposit. BPM MINERALS LTD (ASX: BPM)

Up 117% (18c – 39c) Bulls N’ Bears Runner of the Week is BPM Minerals, which delivered the sort of maiden drilling result that gets rock lickers’ hearts racing. The junior goldie made a cracking high-grade greenfields gold discovery in the first two holes ever drilled at its Bonnie & Clyde Prospect, part of the Forelands gold project in WA’s Eastern Goldfields.

Advertisement

The hits came from a sprawling six-kilometre-long gold-in-soil anomaly. After punching through 15 to 30 metres of paleochannel sands, the company says the bit intersected the richly mineralised metamorphic basement, with one hole returning two standout intervals of 4m at a whopping 20.57 grams per tonne (g/t) gold from 39m, including a bonanza one metre at 73.33g/t, followed by 8m at 9.23g/t from 71m. The second hole failed to return anything significant, but one maiden hole like that is plenty for the market to stew about. The company says its gold sits in an oxidised, quartz-veined shear zone along the Yellow Dam shear, where a major structural flexure appears to have created a prime trap for mineralisation. Management says the host rocks are the same broad geological setting as AngloGold Ashanti’s multi-million-ounce Tropicana deposit, giving the discovery some serious regional credentials. Better still, the shallow mineralisation remains open along strike and down-dip, two of the sweetest words in the exploration business. For a company built around the broader Forelands project, the timing was perfect, with gold surging back above US$4000 an ounce.

Advertisement

BPM says it has completed 38 reverse circulation (RC) holes for 5272m at Bonnie & Clyde, with samples from dozens of them due through the December quarter and into early 2027. A further 27 holes for 4700m remain in the 65-hole program, with diamond drilling now lined up to define the system’s direction beneath the cover. Drilling continues across four priority gold-in-soil anomalies, with BPM holding a handy $5.3 million in the bank to keep the rods turning. For a greenfields discovery made in just its first two holes, Bonnie & Clyde has certainly lived up to its name, with potentially plenty more mischief lurking beneath the sands. NextDC’s S3 headquarters in Artarmon, Sydney. NEXTDC LIMITED (ASX: NXT)

Up 77% ($5.87 – $10.38)

Advertisement

Snagging silver on the week was NEXTDC, proving one man’s trash is another man’s treasure. Barely two weeks after the data centre giant lost roughly $3 billion in valuation in a day as delays forced it to put new developments on ice, the Americans came shopping. Australia’s largest data centre operator now has potential suitors following an aftermarket share raid by the Ackland Investments No.1 Trust, a vehicle owned in equal shares by ASX-listed Goodman Group and US-listed Digital Realty Trust. The pair went after up to 9.9 per cent of the register at A$9.50 a share, a 45 per cent premium to the previous close, with NEXTDC’s board calling it an “opportunistic” attack. While the buyers say they have no current plans for a full takeover bid, they have reserved the right to make one. A strategic block like that tends to put a company in play and with the annual general meeting around the corner, the timing makes interesting reading. It’s a prize worth chasing. NEXTDC is recognised for the design, construction and operation of Australia’s only network of top-tier data centre facilities and is one of the first data centre operators in the Southern Hemisphere. Morgan Stanley reckons the A$9.50 price is below what it would cost to replace the capacity - very opportunistic indeed.

Advertisement

With much of America’s data centre build-out potentially going on pause after the midterms, perhaps a data centre hopeful abroad is the play. There’s no takeover yet, but shareholders, now looking at a stock north of $10, will be waiting eagerly. The question is whether the Yanks will pay up. SCIDEV LTD (ASX: SDV)

Up 48% (14.5c – 21.5c) Rounding out the podium on another quiet and red week for the market was environmental solutions dynamo SciDev, after it was awarded a deal to supply bulk completion chemistry to one of North America’s leading oil and gas producers in the Delaware Basin, a sub-basin of the Permian. Revenue is estimated at up to A$20 million over 12 months, with A$14 million of that landing in FY27, based on the customer’s current expected volumes. The catch is that there’s no minimum purchase commitment, so actual revenue and timing depend on customer orders. It’s a ceiling, not a guarantee, but a handy ceiling nonetheless. The deal extends SciDev’s long-standing relationship with a key energy services customer, providing a platform to expand its products and services over time. The company’s field chemistry team will work alongside the customer’s crew, with dedicated on-site technical support in the mighty Texas basin.

Advertisement

For a company known for water-treatment chemistry, it’s a push further into the oil patch. It builds on three separate contracts secured last month with a total committed value of almost A$8 million. From supplying water-treatment chemistries used in mineral processing, tailings management and industrial wastewater treatment, the order book has morphed to customers across mining, utilities and infrastructure. Those contracts carry extension options worth up to A$4 million, with around A$5 million of revenue expected in FY27. And if the oil and gas game delivers, as it so often can, the rewards could be substantially more. With oil still hovering near US$98 a barrel, the Permian isn’t short of reasons to keep pumping and SciDev is hopeful it can sell the chemistry that helps it do so. Australian shares have limped across the finish line but notched a second straight week of gains, despite facing a slew of domestic and global risks. The S&P/ASX200 fell 44.3 points on Friday, down 0.49 per cent, to 9020.8, as the broader All Ordinaries lost 60.5 points, or 0.66 per cent, to 9144.7. Sharemarkets worldwide felt pressure from continued drops for companies that benefited from the boom in the artificial-intelligence technology industry. AP The top-200 was still up 1.2 one per cent since Monday and has risen for five of the past six weeks, despite the Reserve Bank hiking the official cash rate to 4.85 per cent on Tuesday, its highest level since 2008. The Australian dollar is buying 69 US cents, down from 70.09 US cents on Thursday at 5pm.

Advertisement

Mining stocks eased from Thursday’s surge, tracking tumbling US tech stocks as traders mulled the US midterms’ likely impact on the artificial intelligence build-out that has supported 2026 stock prices and driven Wall Street’s bull market. Related Article Data centres Aftermarket raid: Embattled data centre company NextDC’s shares soar Miners fell taking heavyweights like BHP (down 2.34 per cent), Rio Tinto (-2.03 per cent) and Fortescue (-2 per cent) lower. Gold miners also slumped, with Northern Star sliding 1.12 per cent and Evolution 2.64 per cent lower. Technology stocks fell on the back of the meltdown on Wall Street’s Nasdaq index. Megaport initially tumbled 9.5 per cent but clawed back to end the day down 3.89 per cent. Codan closed 2.9 per cent lower. But Xero and Australia’s most valuable tech company WiseTech retreated by less than 1 per cent. Most financial stocks helped lift the bourse with small gains across the board. Commonwealth Bank added 0.73 per cent, Westpac rose 1.06 per cent, National Australia Bank jumped 2.67 per cent and ANZ added 0.6 per cent. Macquarie Group slumped 3.69 per cent as it was hit with a $100 million capital penalty by financial regulator APRA, saying it breached capital requirements for its non-bank businesses. The wealth giant also reported half-year profits of $2.48 billion.



Advertisement

Energy stocks were largely stable as oil prices advanced overnight after a steep drop in the previous session. In the US, the S&P 500 fell 4.4 per cent for its worst drop since President Donald Trump shook markets worldwide in April 2025 with his “Liberation Day” tariffs. The wipeout more than erased the market’s gain from the day before, which was its best in three months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped more than 1800 points, and the Nasdaq composite tumbled 5.5 per cent. In all, about $US3.2 trillion ($4.6 trillion) was wiped off Wall Street. President Donald Trump lashed out on social media after the brutal Wall Street session. AP Photo/Alex Brandon AI stocks worldwide felt pressure as worries increase about possible moratoriums on data centres following Democratic victories in the US midterm elections. Trump blamed Democrats for the heavy losses in Americans’ 401(k) portfolios – similar to Australia’s superannuation system – as the selloff in technology and artificial intelligence-related stocks deepened after his Republican Party suffered widespread losses in the midterm elections.

“Such a sad thing to watch!” the president said in a post on his Truth Social platform after the close. “It took us so much work to get us to a level that no one has ever seen before, and then this.”

Advertisement

The nationwide victories by Democrats raised the possibility that governments could force pauses in construction of more data centres. That would mean fewer purchases of AI chips, not to mention electricity and other products and services that are getting vacuumed up in the AI frenzy and driving much of the US economy’s growth. Nvidia fell 9.3 per cent and was by far the heaviest weight on the S&P 500, a day after dropping 3.2 per cent. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 17.3 per cent. CoreWeave, a company that rents access to AI chips to customers over the cloud, fell 9.8 per cent. AI chip stocks are some of Wall Street’s most influential because they’ve become some of the largest. Stock prices tend to follow where corporate profits and interest rates go over the long term, depending on them much more than on who controls what in Washington. The capital-raising circus delivered another golden fortnight, with Canaccord Genuity muscling into $262 million worth of gold placements, while rival brokers collected handsome commissions and smaller deals, all of which produced enough options to keep the corporate jocks’ calculators working overtime. Canaccord secured four mandates, Euroz Hartleys featured on three raisings worth $242 million and Argonaut collected two covering $122 million. The figures represent total deal values rather than amounts exclusively allocated to each broker. The Cap Raise Crucible examines a $282 million gold-raising spree, with Canaccord, Argonaut and Euroz Hartleys all enjoying fat broker commissions and the growing divide between placement winners and losers. SCP Resource Finance, Taylor Collison, Morgans and Shaw and Partners joined the picnic, while Mahe Capital, Oakley Capital Partners, AE Advisors Group and 62 Capital demonstrated that modest raisings could produce ambitious remuneration. Across the wider gold sector, announced raisings and offers totalled $282 million. The total also includes $11 million in targeted share purchase plans, still to be banked.

The aftermarket told a different story from the broker sales pitch. Three big gold deals were more than 20 per cent above issue price, while smaller placements and an IPO had punters reaching for the smelling salts. Welcome back to the Cap Raise Crucible. The extensive core yard at Turaco Gold’s 4.6-million-ounce Afema gold project in southeast Côte d’Ivoire. TURACO GOLD (ASX: TCG) Raised: $120 million

Issue price: 60c

Discount: 12.4%

Return against issue: +20.8%

Turaco supplied the heavyweight transaction, with Canaccord and SCP Resource Finance sharing joint lead-manager and bookrunner duties, supported by Euroz Hartleys and Jett Capital as co-managers. The disclosed five per cent cash fee on the first $97.1 million tranche alone represents a whopping $4.855 million commission pool. That figure does not include fees on the balance. Enough to make even a battle-hardened corporate jock reach for the Dom. The proceeds will help consolidate ownership of Turaco’s 4.65-million-ounce Afema gold project in Côte d’Ivoire, including a proposed US$30 million (A$42.7M) payment for Sodim Limited’s remaining 20 per cent stake. The fresh funds will bankroll exploration, pre-development and a definitive feasibility study targeted for the June quarter of 2027. Unlike some recent heavyweight gold raisings — I’m looking at you, Wiluna — Turaco shareholders have something to celebrate. At 72.5 cents, placement subscribers were 20.8 per cent ahead.

The syndicate secured a 0.5 per cent management fee across $82 million and a 4.5 per cent selling fee on the $52 million excluding Genesis - that’s roughly $2.75 million in aggregate cash commissions on my abacus. Brightstar will direct proceeds towards Sandstone, where the Two Mile Hill-Shillington resource has doubled to 1.45 million ounces following the deeper Shirvington discovery. Drilling, an underground exploration decline and development studies aim to establish a second production centre alongside its separately funded Goldfields project. At 60.8 cents, placement subscribers were enjoying a 21.6 per cent gain. Another big book, another healthy commission pool and customers unlikely to demand refunds. Issue price: 24c

Premium: 5.5%

Latest share price: 30c

Return against issue: 25%

Skylark demonstrated that a compelling gold story can persuade investors to pay over the odds. The company secured $20 million at 24 cents, a 5.5 per cent premium, with Canaccord and Taylor Collison sharing joint lead-manager duties. PDI Gold committed $5.1 million for a strategic 9.9 per cent stake, while directors tipped in $2.05 million. PDI’s allocation attracted a two per cent fee, eligible institutional subscriptions up to six per cent and director allocations nothing, producing a potential $873,000 commission pool. The $7.85 million first tranche is accompanied by a $12.15 million second tranche requiring shareholder approval. Skylark is looking to lift its stake in Côte d’Ivoire’s 1.2-million-ounce Zaranou gold project from 51 to 90 per cent and accelerate drilling. Despite the premium, shares are trading at 30 cents, leaving placement punters 25 per cent ahead. Somebody must have let the green fairies out of the absinthe bottle!

Advertisement

Tesoro Gold’s1.93-million-ounce El Zorro gold project in Chile. Canaccord’s golden run extended to Tesoro Gold, joining Morgans as joint lead manager on a $40 million placement at 73 cents. Argonaut and Euroz Hartleys co-managed, with two per cent management and three per cent selling fees, potentially delivering a $2 million commission pool. The money will advance engineering, permitting and feasibility studies at its 1.93-million-ounce El Zorro gold project in Chile. At 74 cents, Tesoro subscribers were barely above water. Meanwhile, not every big cheque needed a broking syndicate.

Advertisement

Centaurus Metals secured US$40 million (A$57M) in strategic equity commitments from Glencore and China’s CNGR for its Jaguar nickel project in Brazil. Both agreed to subscribe at 42.5 cents, a five per cent premium to the 20-day volume-weighted average price. The first US$25 million (A$35.63M) has been banked, with US$15 million (A$21.4M) conditional on shareholder approval and a final investment decision. CNGR’s outstanding US$7.5 million (A$10.7M) also requires Chinese regulatory clearance. No placement broker featured, although Standard Chartered Bank earns 1.5 per cent of CNGR’s equity subscription, potentially US$300,000 (A$427,500) on its full US$20 million (A$28.5M) commitment. At 35.5 cents, the strategic entry price was 16.5 per cent above market. Apparently, even Glencore gets no free pass. At the smaller end of the scale, BOA Resources raised $9.245 million at 10.5 cents through BW Equities and Cygnet Capital, with Bell Potter co-managing. The six per cent commission represented approximately $550,000, while BOA’s 10-cent price left subscribers 4.8 per cent underwater.

Advertisement

Accelerate Resources raised $1.045 million at 0.4 cents through Leeuwin Wealth, whose six per cent fee delivered $62,700. Enough for a six-litre Imperial of 1982 Château Pétrus around the desk. The money will advance the company’s manganese exploration at Woodie Woodie North in the Pilbara. At 0.4 cents, punters were square - no Pétrus, no Panadol and no gain. The rights-issue market offered brokers other ways to make a quid. ADX Energy launched a renounceable entitlement offer seeking up to $5.2 million at 1.2 cents for its Austrian oil and gas portfolio.

Advertisement

Mahe Capital partially underwrote $1 million, earning a five per cent underwriting fee worth $50,000, plus management and qualifying shortfall-placement fees. The proposed package also included up to 20.81 million underwriter options exercisable at 2.5 cents until December 2028, separate from shareholder options. Not bad for underwriting a lazy million. ADX traded at 1.1 cents, 8.3 per cent below the still-open offer. Perth-based biotech Proteomics International offered a contrast, launching a share purchase plan seeking up to $5 million at 10 cents. No broker needed for that one. Shareholders were offered one free option for every new share, exercisable at 15 cents until November 2028, subject to approval. Proceeds will accelerate commercialisation of its diagnostic technology targeting diabetic kidney disease, oesophageal cancer and endometriosis through Healius in Australia, and support preparations for US expansion. At 9.4 cents, the market price stood six per cent below the offer.

Advertisement

While one company offered underwriting fees and broker options, the other went directly to shareholders. Which approach would punters prefer? Pinnacle Minerals flagged a $1.3 million raise at 4.5 cents, with Oakley Capital Partners and AE Advisors Group sharing lead-manager and adviser duties. The six per cent cash fee is worth up to $78,000. Hardly enough to trouble Collins Street. But that was just the entrée. The proposed package also included 3.33 million facilitation shares, 3.33 million facilitation performance shares and 22 million adviser performance rights, subject to approvals and hurdles. More than 28 million potential securities on top of a cash commission feels like a hefty remuneration package against just $1.3 million in fresh funding. Pinnacle’s 4.2-cent share price was 6.7 per cent below the proposed issue price.

Advertisement

However, the options cupboard was not finished being raided. Perth-based 62 Capital lined up a $1 million placement for Simble Solutions at 0.35 cents a share, pocketing a six per cent cash commission worth $60,000 and potentially another 50 million broker options, exercisable at 0.7 cents over four years, subject to approval. Yep, 50 million! The options require shareholder approval, while Simble’s 0.3-cent share price left placement punters 14.3 per cent underwater. While the broker may have picked up potential upside, the punters are more likely to call for the nurse. Finally, the IPO market delivered its own cold shower. Jacaranda Natural Resources raised $8 million at 20 cents, with Gaia Natural Capital acting as joint lead manager and sole bookrunner alongside Boston Global. The prospectus provided for a two per cent management fee, four per cent selling fee on eligible subscriptions and a $50,000 completion fee.

Advertisement

Depending on eligible allocations, cash remuneration totalled between $370,000 and $530,000, with Gaia also entitled to 1.6 million lead-manager options exercisable at 30 cents over three years. A handy collection of incentives for an $8 million float. Jacaranda traded at 18 cents, 10 per cent below its IPO price, after a recent intraday plunge to 12.5 cents — a stomach-churning 37.5 per cent below the float price. At least punters have likely climbed back off the ledge. As usual, the brokers got their share. Investors, meanwhile, have their work cut out.

I think [jockey] Alysha [Collett] will have some hope of doing that because in a race they go a bit quicker than a trial.

“I’ve got 30-odd babies and I’ve got to start somewhere, so I’ve been trialling a lot of them and tipping them out, but I’m a private trainer and the boss wants to see a couple run, so this bloke is going to the races. “He’s showing us something, but I need him to drop his head. It’s so hard to overrace and still win races. I haven’t seen many do it. I’ve seen a couple, but they were champions. But generally you are using too much petrol. “I just want to see him drop his head, if he does that, I’ll be tickled pink.” Geoff Allendorf pictured in 1981. “I’ve never been associated with older horses because every good young horse I’ve handled has either been retired or sold,” Allendorf said at the time. Fairfax Preparing two-year-olds is a new test for Allendorf, who has called on his early experiences as a jockey to meet the challenge. He carved out a career in Sydney in the 1970s and ’80s before riding for three years in Hong Kong then moving to Macau, where he later transitioned to training. His 19-year training career ended in 2024 when racing ceased in Macau.

Advertisement

After staying on in Macau to help rehome and transport horses, Allendorf returned to Australia but had no thoughts of training again, before a call came about the Mathland opportunity on Caulfield Cup day last year from mate Kenny Man, who had trained for YP Cheng. Now Allendorf is navigating new territory. “Before this, when I trained in Asia, we never dealt with two-year-olds. Even in Hong Kong, they are all older horses, three-year-old plus,” he said. “Luckily, I rode a lot of two-year-olds for good trainers, so that gives me a good insight to it. I think I probably won about half of the lead-up races to the Slipper, and for different trainers, from Terry Ramsey to [Geoff] ‘Doc’ Chapman. “I was riding their trackwork, too, so I’ve got some idea how to treat them.”

Advertisement

Allendorf is following Bart Cummings’ philosophy of patience being key, with his larger-than-expected team. Related Article Horse racing Failed legal battle to retain independence costs cash-strapped ATC $4.1m “I’m getting on in age, so I’ve got patience. I’m not in a hurry,” he said. “I’ve had a bit of success in Macau, and I want to have success here, but you can’t make it happen, you’ve got to let it happen. “People keep saying to me, ‘You haven’t had any winners,’ but I haven’t had many starters.

Advertisement

“The boss gave me half a dozen horses and said ‘I’ll buy you 10’, so that’s 16 in my arithmetic, but I’ve got probably 40. He went to the sales and went berserk. “But I’ve got some nice ones and some cheap ones I really like. I’m hoping by January, I’m up and going with a good half a dozen two-year-olds, and four or five three-year-olds.”

NationalDavid Jones collapse Editorial The demise of David Jones leaves an empty feeling The Herald's View Editorial November 6, 2026 — 4:47pm

November 6, 2026 — 4:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The black-and-white houndstooth print on a David Jones bag has been a badge of honour for generations of Australians. For many, growing up in the suburbs meant a train trip to the city for school uniforms or, come December, the window display and Santa, and lunch in the food hall. Dressed in their best clothes, children wandered the floors of this bastion of middle-class refinement with mothers who inspected and touched the racks of leading Australian fashion labels and had their own dreams. The iconic retailer was renowned for its lavish window displays and houndstooth shopping bags. Jessica Hromas Prue Acton, Sportscraft and Carla Zampatti were joined by the best global labels and, together with seasonal shows replete with big names on the runway and celebrity guests, made David Jones Australia’s fashion central. It was more than a shopping emporium too. The David Jones Art Gallery supported Australian artists; before television arrived in the 1950s, a staff amateur theatre group, the Dajonian Repertory Society, staged six plays a year; on her first visit to Sydney in 1954, Queen Elizabeth II attended a banquet dinner on the seventh floor of the Elizabeth Street store.

Advertisement

But after 188 years, David Jones’ future hangs in the balance, with the board calling in administrators and the lender sending in the receivers. The department store chain is still trading, but no one is sure for how long. David Jones employs about 6000 staff and has 38 physical stores, with 17 of those in Westfield shopping centres. Unions are concerned about layoffs before Christmas. Suppliers are under no delusions. Various businesses have been left in the lurch and the owners and agents of luxury brands have began removing stock from outlets where they have “concession pad” agreements with the store. The collapse is part of a worldwide phenomenon – department stores have been smashed by an alarming combination: the global financial crisis, the COVID-19 pandemic, the ongoing cost-of-living crisis; and, most painfully, the rapid rise of online shopping. They have also been hit by what’s termed the bifurcation of retail, where top-end shoppers have migrated to super-luxe stores and the bottom end of the market hunts for more bargain-basement offerings, with department stores taking the hit in the middle. David Jones’ problems were compounded by dubious business decisions that began during the 1980s takeover fad with the Jones family selling out, and continued on and off for years until the company was unable to pay rent to Westfield last September.

Advertisement

Twelve years ago, a South African company reportedly paid $2.1 billion to buy David Jones. Three years ago, Anchorage Capital Partners bought the department store chain for less than $100 million but still could not make a go of it. Related Article David Jones collapse Six things to know about David Jones on the brink It is a long way from 1838, when Welsh draper David Jones opened one of the world’s first department stores in Sydney. It remained largely a Sydney phenomenon for the first century or so, opening in Newcastle in 1957 and then expanding into the regions and metropolitan suburbs around the nation. David Jones arrived in Victoria in the 1960s, and in 1982 it acquired the three stores of Buckley & Nunn located in Bourke Street, Northland and Chadstone. In 1987, David Jones purchased the former GJ Coles store and building at 299 Bourke Street, Melbourne, converting it into a David Jones store. David Jones had always been Sydney’s most upmarket store, specialising in quality goods and elite customer services.

Advertisement

But in Melbourne, David Jones was slightly lower down the pecking order. Georges Store in Collins Street had long catered to the cream of Melbourne society and liked to think of itself as the equal to Harrods of London. In 1981, David Jones bought Georges and slowly squeezed it into oblivion, eventually closing it in 1995 in the hope of keeping much of the cream for itself. It did not happen. In the end, David Jones was slowly squeezed by rising costs, changing shopping habits and online technology, a vestige of a way of shopping out of step with the times. The sun is setting on an Australian retail icon. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up for our Opinion newsletter.

title: From Swans to the AFL’s ugly ducklings: Sydney’s shame is no one-off
text:
Advertisement

SportAFLAFL 2026 Opinion From Swans to the AFL’s ugly ducklings: Sydney’s shame is no one-off Jake Niall Chief football writer, The Age November 6, 2026 — 4:25pm

November 6, 2026 — 4:25pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

That the Sydney Swans have vowed to change, to repair the damage wrought by the Pullman hotel scandal and Tom Papley’s alleged drug offence, confirms that they know something is genuinely amiss in their playing group. One way to view their far-reaching “examination” is that it represents a kind of cultural audit in which they are seeking to answer to this question – What are the underlying factors that have seen senior players make such poor and reckless choices? Tom Papley became a pin-up player for the Swans after the Pullman hotel scandal, but that has now changed. Steven Siewert Papley’s roadside drug test failure – the outcome of which is yet to be verified by a secondary sample – can be a positive for the Swans, so to speak, if it forces them to confront the root causes of the Pullman fiasco. Until Papley’s arrest, it was possible for the club to consider the Pullman as an anomaly – players took liberties, made terrible and unprofessional choices and embarrassed themselves and the club (and possibly crossed legal and ethical lines), but that this was out of collective character.

Advertisement

When the Swans responded so magnificently to the Pullman scandal on the field, by slaying the Brisbane Lions in that extraordinary qualifying final and then running Fremantle to the wire in the prelim, despite a scandal-depleted side, it was natural to think that their stirring response, not the Pullman, demonstrated their true cultural colours. The hierarchy’s handling of the Pullman was powerful, too, in that, as chairman Andrew Pridham rightly asserted, they had been willing to torpedo their finals campaign by suspending the five for the remainder of the season. Loading Commendably, they did not follow the expedient old-school footy club script for scandals, in which players would have missed only one or two games (or none) when the grail was within their grasp. It’s worth noting that Papley himself was outstanding in the upset of the Lions, booting five goals. The same senior player who summoned his best in September has subsequently embarrassed everyone with a poor choice (allegedly).

Advertisement

Herein lies the critical distinction that the Swans must surely understand now if they didn’t previously: That committed performance on the field isn’t necessarily conducive to the best behaviours or culture in the outside world. Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Unacceptable and must change’: Swans hierarchy apologise, detail review into their AFL program Footy is replete with the mythology that great teams and players carry some moral purpose, that successful teams – and the Swans are relatively successful, albeit without a recent flag – win games and finals because they have a “good culture”, led by senior players who set foundational standards and lead them not into temptation. Geelong people sometimes spruiked a culture of “character over talent”, which this column considers to be bunkum. The cultural strength of the Cats, as with Collingwood, has been their competitive ethos. They have senior players who refuse to accept defeat. This does not mean they all refuse a drink card or quick buck. The truth is that, just as Shane Warne’s wizardry was immune to whatever missteps he made in his life, football performance is not reflective of cleanskin behaviours outside the field.

Advertisement

It is possible for a team to party hard and still perform. Indeed, there’s a possibility that the Swans’ (relative) success can lead players to entitlement, which, in turn, can spawn a feeling of invincibility, leading you to a hotel room with topless dancers, and whatever mood-altering substances were present (certainly alcohol), at 5am. Wisely, the Sydney board and CEO Matthew Pavlich have engaged an external company, Intersection, to assist them in their examination of club culture, and it is not confined to just the men’s players. They are speaking to the AFLW cohort and commercial partners - some of whom need reassurance. Sydney CEO Matthew Pavlich was forced to face the media again this week as his club found itself embroiled in a new scandal. Sitthixay Ditthavong Another scandal could well cost the Swans millions, just as the Pullman has cost Isaac Heeney a pretty penny in sponsorship. Many of the celebrated club reviews - Geelong (2006), Richmond (2016), Collingwood (2018) - have been focused on the playing group’s failures to achieve their potential, under-performances that were overcome by changes.

Advertisement

This examination (the club is avoiding the R word, review) differs in that the Swans are canvassing other stakeholders. It is not simply about extracting the best output from players on the field. Related Article CBD Latest Sydney Swans scandal means marquee name a late scratching Underlying the club’s self-examination is the fact that the Swans are a distinctive club, with different needs to the majority of AFL clubs. Consider the following unique traits of the Swans: 1. They play in a market where the AFL is not followed so intensely, where it is entertainment more than a binding faith. Players in Randwick and Coogee are left alone and can (and do) have a drink without repercussions.

Advertisement

2. They have a more educated, affluent fan base, in inner Sydney and consequently have more female engagement and a more progressive social flavour (see Pride games). 3. Their AFLW team attracts more interest - crowds are exceptional - and is more central to the club than at many rivals. 4. They have made a virtue, and profited from their purported contrast with the NRL clubs, who are viewed as more old-world and scandal-prone. Emotions were high after Sydney’s stirring qualifying final win over eventual premiers Brisbane in September. AFL Photos via Getty Images To own a fan base that values women – and is less apt to accept the “boys will be boys” excuses – creates a higher demand for more respectful behaviours in that realm; at Sydney, there was immediate condemnation from a hefty section of members when the Pullman incident erupted.

Advertisement

The Sydney hierarchy thus will have to consider whether their men’s playing group is capable of meeting the club’s broader values, in which good citizenship - respectful treatment of women, avoidance of drugs and excessive alcohol consumption and associated anti-social behaviours - is elevated. Related Article AFL 2026 Surprise twist in legal move by dancers against Swans players caught in hotel saga Given that three of the Pullman five and Papley are/were among their most valuable and elite players (counting Nick Blakey), it’s reasonable to question whether there’s a gaping leadership deficit, outside of skipper Callum Mills, who rose to the moment post-Pullman and whose season-long absence due to injury will be a major challenge. Sydney doesn’t need to repair what happens in those two and half crowded hours each week during the AFL season. As with the West Coast Eagles of 2007-08, whose issues (drugs mainly) were far more serious, as Dean Cox would know, and were willing to sacrifice a ladder position in the short-term and some of whom suffered long-term fallout, the change the Swans desire won’t be measured in wins and losses.
