The gates to Melbourne Park will open a day earlier in 2027 – but there will be no Open tournament tennis played. Tennis Australia is badging Saturday, January 10 Kids Tennis Day. Children and families will be encouraged to visit the precinct to watch training and practice matches and pick up a racquet – and, Tennis Australia hopes, buy food, drink and merch. Lleyton Hewitt at the launch of Kids Tennis Day. Zoey Duchene Tennis Australia chief executive Andrew Abdo made the announcement at Melbourne Park, joined by tennis legend Lleyton Hewitt and, mysteriously, a koala and a kangaroo to go with the “Australian-inspired” theme for the 2027 tournament. “It’s an engine that can be used to reinvest back into the sport,” Abdo said. “Having a focus on a dedicated day for kids is symbolically important, but it’s also an opportunity where we might discover the next superhero, and that’s exciting for us.”

Advertisement

Lleyton Hewitt (left), Andrew Abdo and a wildlife carer brought a koala and a kangaroo to Kia Arena. Zoey Duchene The schedule change follows this year’s shift of the Australian Open, which ran from January 12 to February 1 instead of finishing on the Australia Day weekend in late January, as it has in the past. Abdo took over as Tennis Australia chief executive in August after leaving the NRL. This is one of his first major announcements since he got into hot water for getting a player’s name wrong at his first Australian Open launch. Tennis Australia could not give an exact cost for the extra day, but Abdo said it wouldn’t be possible without sponsorship. “There definitely is an investment into it, and it’s an investment we’re happy to make,” Abdo said.

Advertisement

The Australian Open is among the biggest economic drivers in Australian sport. This year’s tournament was estimated to have pumped more than $600 million into the Melbourne economy, according to NAB analysis, a rise of 7 to 10 per cent from 2025. Related Article Australian Open A translucent, climate-controlled dome over Melbourne Park? Tiley’s radical plan to reshape the Australian Open Revenue from the Open has steadily increased since 2010, apart from a three-year slump after COVID. But taxpayers have also helped foot the bill. More than a billion dollars has been spent on upgrading Melbourne Park since 2011, and an agreement between Tennis Australia and the Victorian government keeps the tournament in Melbourne until at least 2046. Growth is also not limited to revenue. Melbourne Park’s annual report shows media reach is vast and still expanding. More than 13 million viewers tuned in to Nine’s coverage in 2025, up from about 12.8 million the year before, while content on the Open’s channels generated 45 million engagements across 7000 posts. (Nine is the owner of this masthead.) Hewitt also supported the push to get more children involved in the sport, saying it was the best way to produce more top-level players like himself and Alex de Minaur.

Advertisement

“We’ve got to work through the pathway, obviously,” Hewitt said. “We’ve got to try and become a real high-performance group ... and try and transition the best kids through.” Hewitt reflected on his 2005 final and the “wave of excitement” from the Australian public, and said he remembered experiencing Kids Tennis Day himself and playing games in Rod Laver Arena. “The more that we can get out there and host Kids Day, put on a good spectacle that people want to be involved with and come out to, I think it helps the sport in Australia,” Hewitt said. Abdo said the 2027 Open was already shaping up to be a strong one. “We are ahead on ticket sales, which is terrific,” he said. “We’ve got more interstate, more international visitors than we’ve had before, which is terrific. The merits of the Australian Turf Club board’s failed battle to retain its independence can now be weighed against a $4.1 million cost after the release of the cash-strapped organisation’s annual report. The ATC, which operates Sydney’s four metropolitan thoroughbred racetracks and owns all of them except Royal Randwick, lost $4.8 million in the 2025-26 financial year, up from $2.6 million in 2024-25. The Australian Turf Club operates the Randwick, Rosehill, Canterbury and Warwick Farm race tracks, and owns all except Randwick. Getty Images However, the deficit for last year would have been about $700,000 if not for the board’s legal costs from its fight to prevent regulator Racing NSW appointing an administrator over concerns about the club’s financial position, which included a $30 million bank loan, and corporate governance. That battle started when Racing NSW issued a show cause notice in September last year, following the sacking of ATC chief executive Matt Galanos and resignation of directors Ben Bayot and Natalie Hewson, and ended in June when the regulator won a NSW Supreme Court appeal to appoint Morgan Kelly as administrator.

Advertisement

The ruling included an order for the ATC to pay the legal costs of Racing NSW, which this week reported an operating surplus of $13.63 million in 2025-26, up from $12.96 million the previous year. Kelly’s review of the ATC started as a consultant in April, under an agreement with Racing NSW to resume its additional funding of the club, and he took over as administrator on July 8, effectively replacing the board. Chairman Tim Hale, vice-chair Caroline Searcy and newest board addition Bernie Brookes became part of advisory subcommittee with Racing NSW directors Simon Tuxen and Michael Crismale. ATC chairman Tim Hale. Steven Siewert Kelly noted in the annual report that the club’s revenue of $379 million was up on 2024-25’s $373.4

million and losses were down without the one-off legal costs, but there was work to do. “While the club’s underlying assets and operations remain strong, the continued loss-making performance highlights the need to strengthen financial and commercial discipline across the organisation,” Kelly wrote.

Advertisement

“Our review to date has identified opportunities to enhance commercial performance, improve operational efficiency and strengthen governance. In a number of areas, costs have increased over time and opportunities to maximise revenue have not been fully realised.” Related Article Horse racing Racing NSW appoints administrator, advisory panel at cash-strapped ATC Sources who spoke on the condition of anonymity have told this masthead the operational efficiencies have not included forced job cuts, but the club has reduced its staff slightly through natural attrition, although roles attached to horse welfare or safety have been untouched. An ongoing court case regarding alleged thefts of cash from raceday safes has not impacted the club, which is insured for those losses. A positive for the club in this year’s report was the absence of an auditor’s notice of concern, present in the previous year’s report, over the ATC’s financial viability.

Advertisement

Members will have the chance to address the club’s situation at the annual general meeting at Royal Randwick on November 26. The ATC board initially succeeded in blocking Racing NSW’s move to appoint Kelly in December before winning again in March when NSW Supreme Court Justice Francois Kunc ruled that the regulator’s move was not authorised under the Thoroughbred Racing Act. However, Racing NSW’s appeal was upheld when the panel found the club’s finances and corporate governance were within the definition of horse racing under the Act.

title: Babies made a comeback – but that was before the latest rate rises
text:

PoliticsFederalBabies Babies made a comeback – but that was before the latest rate rises Matt Wade and Shane Wright Updated November 6, 2026 — 3:52pm ,first published 3:49pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. High inflation and the Reserve Bank’s steep interest rate hikes could halt a small baby bounce with new figures showing a turnaround in Australia’s fertility rate that is being driven by women in regional parts of the country. Figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics, released on Friday, showed there were 299,903 births registered in 2025, a 2.6 per cent lift on the previous year and the biggest one-year increase since the post-Covid baby boom. Loading The increase arrested a long-term fall in the fertility rate which lifted marginally to 1.497 after dropping to a record low in 2024. A fertility rate of 2.1 is needed to naturally replace a nation’s population. It is the third consecutive year that it has been below 1.5. The fertility rate fell in every capital city bar Hobart, with the biggest declines in Perth, Brisbane and Adelaide which all recorded sharp increases in home prices through 2025. The lowest capital city fertility rate is in Canberra at just 1.29.

Advertisement

Advertisement

In the City of Melbourne the fertility rate was just 0.5, the lowest of any local government area in the nation. Other Melbourne LGAs with very low fertility rates were Yarra (0.79), Port Phillip (0.81) and Stonnington (0.81). But cheaper regional areas have much higher fertility rates with some areas actually going through a modest baby boom. In regional NSW the number of births jumped by 8 per cent in 2025 and the fertility rate was a relatively healthy 1.87. The fertility rate in regional Victoria was 1.91. Across regional Victoria, councils such as Swan Hill, Southern Grampians, Moyne and Moira have fertility rates above 2.1 which held steady or improved through 2025. In NSW, centres such as Cowra, Dubbo, Griffith and Yass also held fertility rates above replacement level.

Advertisement

KPMG urban economist Terry Rawnsley attributed Australia’s modest “baby bounce” in 2025 to improvements in the economic circumstances of families in that period. “There was a bit of an improvement in cost of living pressures at the back end of 2023 and in 2024…and interest rates were kind of softening a bit at that time, so people had the confidence to press go on the family and we’ve seen that baby bounce come through in 2025,” he said. “It shows a clear pattern between households’ disposable income and their propensity to have children.” But that could come to an end.

Advertisement

Inflation has climbed to 4.3 per cent, in part due to high oil prices, prompting the Reserve Bank to lift official rates five times this year. On a $600,000 mortgage, the rate rises will add about $500 to monthly repayments while higher petrol prices are costing households around $100 a month more. Rawnsley said rising cost of living pressures this year would likely put downward pressure on birth numbers. “Crystal balling for the next year’s numbers, we’ll probably see another dip as people feel squeezed by cost of living,” he said. Related Article Australian economy What is a recession and are we in one? A bluffer’s guide Rawnsley said the national fertility rate has now hovered around the 1.5 mark for the past three years.

Advertisement

“The fertility rate seems to have found a bit of a floor in the past few years but there’s no clear factor that might drive it back-up again towards the levels around 1.7 we had pre-COVID,” he said. “There’s no big policy lever or change pointing to a turning around.” The fertility slump is not unique to Australia – many nations in Europe and parts of Asia have had far steeper declines, triggering warnings of a “demographic winter” in some. Opposition leader Angus Taylor, a father of four, said a lift in hope could help boost the chances of more children. “For young Australians to want to have a family, they’ve got to have hope. They’ve got to believe that the economy gives them opportunities,” he said. The ABS figures showed fertility among young women continues to fall, hitting record lows among teenagers and those aged between 20 and 24. The lift in 2025 fertility rates was driven by women aged between 25 and 39. There were 4148 births of twins and 46 triplets or more, in line with previous years.

Shareholders of Australia’s largest media company, Nine Entertainment, have delivered a strike against its remuneration report and chief executive Matt Stanton’s pay, after the company’s share price slumped 30 per cent in the past year. Company chair Peter Tonagh defended Stanton’s record as chief executive after two influential proxy advisory firms, CGI Glass Lewis and ISS urged investors to vote against the company’s executive pay arrangements, in part because Nine is now a smaller business after selling Domain last year. Tonagh rejected those calls, saying Stanton should not be punished for selling the digital real estate listings business and buying outdoor media firm QMS. The company will take the strike seriously, however, he said. Nine CEO Matt Stanton (right) at the AGM on Friday. The company’s remuneration report was hit with a second strike in three years. AAPIMAGE “Our perspective as a board is the argument that we should reduce Matt’s salary because he did a good job of selling a business and returning value to shareholders, and buying another one, which requires more work from him, is an argument that is not persuasive to us,” Tonagh said while fronting his first annual general meeting as chair of Nine.

Advertisement

The comments came during a meeting that was repeatedly sidetracked by a raft of eccentric questions from a number of retail investors, covering topics including the limited biscuit selection for shareholders and why the company doesn’t use AI to audit its finances. “I notice in the foyer itself, all we’ve got is a tray of biscuits bought from local Metro and nothing more. I mean, things are not aligning, and you’re saving money by holding in these cramped little quarters. So that surely be an incentive to give something a bit more generously,” one of the elderly investors said. He was then backed up by another investor, who said the company had a “lousy reputation” for its hospitality spread for investors, failing to provide sandwiches or sushi. Retail investors made their thoughts known about NIne’s ‘lousy’ selection of biscuits and food. Stanton’s base pay was $1.6 million last financial year and his total remuneration, including bonuses, was $3 million, according to Nine’s annual report.

title: More than three months after the World Cup, why haven't the Socceroos been paid?
text:
in brief Some Socceroos are still chasing Football Australia for 2026 FIFA World Cup pay.

The team has also petitioned have their match in Jordan moved due to the war in the Middle East.

Socceroos players who competed at this year's FIFA World Cup in North America are yet to be paid their match fees, three months after the tournament finished.

Just days after it was revealed that both male and female national team players were taking legal action against Football Australia (FA) over their revenue-sharing agreement, members of the 2026 Socceroos World Cup squad are pursuing Australia's football governing body for match payments.

Payment was due within a fortnight of the date they broke camp.

Australia were knocked out of the tournament at the round-of-32 stage in a loss to Egypt on 3 July.

FA, which recorded a $23 million loss over the last two financial years, said tax complications in the United States caused the delay.

The body said it was working with the players' union, Professional Footballers Australia (PFA), to "resolve the outstanding matters as quickly as possible" and that it was ready to make the payments.

"Before those payments can be processed, however, we require final specialist advice on the North American taxation obligations applicable to the payments, as well as some further player distribution information being provided through the PFA," FA said in a statement.

"Recognising the complexity of North American taxation requirements, FIFA facilitated access to specialist tax support for all participating member associations to help them understand and meet their respective obligations.

READ MORE Asian Cup postponed for 11 months due to conflict in the Middle East

"We have been actively engaging with those specialist advisers since the World Cup to confirm the applicable tax and withholding treatment."

If a player sees game time, or is an unused substitute for the national team, they earn around $6,000 in match fees.

The Socceroos played two friendlies against Mexico and Switzerland before three World Cup group games and the Egypt shootout defeat, meaning players named for all six games are heading into camp this week out of pocket by roughly $36,000.

There were no known payment issues for the four friendlies which took place in the US in the October and November windows last year.

READ MORE Socceroos' next test to go ahead despite Saudi Arabia airport attacks

PFA chief executive Beau Busch said the situation was unacceptable.

"Any matter related to international tax was foreseeable and should have been addressed long before a ball was kicked at the tournament," he said.

Members of the squad who faced Brazil in two friendlies in Queensland in September are understood to have been paid in full.

Socceroos petition for Jordan match to move

FA's delay in paying World Cup match fees comes as players head into November's friendly window in the Middle East.

Some players have expressed concerns about travelling to the region — Australia will face Qatar in Doha and Jordan in Amman — amid the wider conflict.

The purpose of those friendlies in the current climate has been brought into question since the Asian Football Confederation opted to delay the Asian Cup.

Socceroos players, via their union, have urged FA to reschedule or relocate their upcoming friendly against Jordan in Amman due to safety concerns.

The Asian Football Confederation postponed that tournament, originally scheduled for January-February in Saudi Arabia, following the attack on Riyadh's international airport by Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen.

The Socceroos squad was expected to be named on Friday, but the announcement has been pushed back to the weekend amid uncertainty over whether some players will withdraw.

Indonesia's football association has already cancelled a 13 November planned friendly against Jordan in Amman amid an escalation in violence in the area, and the PFA made it clear Australian players didn't want to proceed.

"The PFA has worked with Football Australia over recent weeks in relation to security concerns regarding the upcoming assembly and engaged its own independent security experts," Busch said.

"With the full support of the PFA, the players have overwhelmingly expressed their view that the Jordan match should be rescheduled or relocated.

"We are committed to working with FA to reach a sensible solution."

title: These Kiwis were driven to Australia by rising costs. Could an election bring them home?
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Despite working fewer hours and earning less, the Ririnui family has more money left over each week on the Gold Coast than they did in Auckland.

Tajai Ririnui, 32, her husband, and three daughters moved from New Zealand just three months ago after struggling to make ends meet amid a cost of living crisis that showed little sign of easing.

"After rent, fuel, kindy, groceries and putting money aside for things like power, water and internet, we were left with next to nothing," she tells SBS News.

"Don't get me wrong, we had everything we needed, but there was no room to save, no room for extra activities with our girls and very little opportunity to actually enjoy life.”

Ririnui's husband Jayden, 31, worked in floor restoration in New Zealand, putting in 12-hour days, sometimes six or seven days a week, to support the family. He now works as a scaffolder on the Gold Coast.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We're averaging below what we were getting in New Zealand, but we have more left over, which is ironic because we're working less," Tajai says.

The pull home is very strong, but honestly, you'd rather … have everything and that little bit more here than be broke and have nothing at home.

Tajai Ririnui and her family moved to the Gold Coast due to the high cost of living in New Zealand. Source: Supplied

The Ririnuis are not alone.

Australia's higher wages and broader employment opportunities have long drawn New Zealanders across the Tasman, where they can live and work indefinitely under the Trans-Tasman Travel Arrangement. The movement has continued even as the economic gap between the two countries has fluctuated over time.

In the year to March 2026, an estimated 47,900 New Zealanders moved to Australia, while about 19,900 New Zealanders moved in the opposite direction, leaving a net migration loss of about 27,900 people, according to Stats NZ.

But beyond the headline migration figures, new research suggests more young New Zealanders are leaving for Australia and elsewhere overseas for the long term, raising concerns about the country's economic future.

As New Zealanders prepare to vote in Saturday's general election, the question is whether the next government can turn the tide and convince more of them to stay.

Why Kiwis are leaving

Former New Zealand prime minister Jacinda Ardern renewed attention on the country's emigration debate when she settled on Sydney's Northern Beaches earlier this year.

She joined the nearly 620,000 New Zealand-born people already living in Australia as of 2024 — representing about one in eight Kiwis.

Source: SBS News

The number of arrivals ebbs and flows depending on how each country's economy is performing. But a new report suggests more young people are making the move with little intention of returning.

About 77,500 New Zealanders aged 18 to 30 left the country long term for Australia and elsewhere between 2023 and 2025 — 60 per cent above the pre-pandemic average — according to Victor Consulting research commissioned by New Zealand's Green Party.

Of those who left, more than four in 10 are not expected to return, according to the research, potentially resulting in the permanent loss of NZ$12 billion ($9.7 billion) in education and healthcare investment.

Paul Spoonley, a New Zealand sociologist and emeritus professor at Massey University, says young New Zealanders have traditionally left in two groups: school leavers and graduates in their mid-20s.

He links the recent departures to graduates struggling to find work in New Zealand while Australian employers actively recruit, particularly in health and policing.

The Auckland skyline. The number of arrivals from New Zealand to Australia often depends on how each economy is performing. Source: Bloomberg / Becki Moss

Historically, around half of New Zealanders who moved to Australia eventually returned to New Zealand, but Spoonley suspects a larger share of the current wave may stay overseas.

"What we'd normally expect is that as the economic conditions in New Zealand improve over the medium to short, long term, then the migration would ease," he tells SBS News.

But I'm not sure that those economic conditions in New Zealand are going to be as short-term as we thought.

New Zealand has experienced a years-long economic downturn, with two recessions since 2022. Although the economy has begun to recover, unemployment remains elevated at 5.7 per cent, an 11-year high, compared with 4.7 per cent in Australia.

Last month, New Zealand finance minister Nicola Willis announced the National Party's election commitments to encourage young Kiwis to stay or return home. These include plans to legislate for lower student loan repayments, expand a 5 per cent home deposit scheme and extend paid parental leave, if the coalition government is returned to office.

But New Zealand economist Shamubeel Eaqub is sceptical there is an easy solution to stemming the flow of people overseas, pointing to four decades of faster wage growth in Australia.

Economist Shamubeel Eaqub says there are no easy solutions to entice New Zealanders to stay. Source: Supplied

In 2009, then prime minister John Key set a target of closing the income gap with Australia by 2025 — a goal that was never met.

"Obviously, we didn't, and so therein lies the issue. Politicians have learned from that a little bit, and they're less gung-ho about proclaiming they're going to somehow close the gap with Australia," Eaqub tells SBS News.

The cost of staying

Another New Zealander planning to make the move is Lisa Robb, 47, who has lived in Katikati, a town of 6,000 people roughly two hours' drive south-east of Auckland, with her family for 23 years.

After work dried up for her husband Manny's plastering business, he moved to Perth in February.

Lisa Robb (third from the left) is planning to join her husband, Manny (third from the right), in Perth after her youngest son finishes school. Source: Supplied

In New Zealand, he often worked seven days a week. In Perth, he now earns three times as much while working Monday to Friday, Robb says.

Two of her adult children have already moved to Australia in search of better opportunities, as have her stepson and his young family.

She plans to join them after her 15-year-old son finishes school.

"You just don't get to live a life because you're too busy working to make the money that you need just to survive, not even thrive, just survive," Robb tells SBS News.

"We wouldn't even have considered it if we didn't need to."

I love my country … I love the culture here, I love my trees and my birds, and all the rest of it, but if you can't afford to live then you can't afford to live.

While some inflationary pressures, including global energy and commodity price shocks, are beyond the government's control, Robb believes domestic policy could do more to ease the pressure on households.

"If they want people to stop leaving New Zealand, then they have to make New Zealand a more attractive place to live and at the moment, New Zealand isn't an attractive place to live," she says.

"I don't know what the answer is ... I just know that I live here, and I have to pay my bills, and I can't afford to do that because of how expensive things are."

While economic factors remain the biggest driver of emigration, Mark Berger, who runs relocation company NZ Relo, says families are often chasing something harder to measure.

Source: SBS News

"It's all about hope … it's someone thinking about their future and how they can apply it to better their family and their circumstances," he tells SBS News.

A knife-edge contest

Saturday's election is shaping up as a tight contest, with Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's National Party polling at 30 per cent and the opposition Labour Party, led by former prime minister Chris Hipkins, on 29 per cent, according to the latest 1News Verian poll.

Government coalition parties ACT New Zealand and New Zealand First polled 10 per cent and 8 per cent respectively, leaving the right-wing bloc with a projected 58 seats — three short of the 61 needed for a majority in New Zealand's 120-seat parliament.

National Party leader Christopher Luxon (centre) has promised to cut government spending if re-elected. Source: Getty / Hagen Hopkins

The left-wing bloc, comprising Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori (the Māori Party), would secure 56 or 60 seats, depending on the outcome of the Māori electorate contests and potential parliamentary overhangs.

The poll also puts the Opportunity Party on 6 per cent, potentially giving it seven MPs and a significant say in post-election coalition negotiations. Neither major bloc is projected to secure a majority on its own.

The election is being fought against a backdrop of mounting pressure on household budgets.

An Ipsos poll released last week found 64 per cent of respondents believed the cost of living was the country's biggest issue, followed by healthcare at 45 per cent, fuel prices (31 per cent), the economy (30 per cent) and unemployment (19 per cent).

While inflation has eased from its post-pandemic peak, it remained at 3.7 per cent in the 12 months to September, above the Reserve Bank's target range of 1 to 3 per cent. Although down from 4.1 per cent in the year to June, many households have yet to experience sustained relief.

National's approach to tackling the cost of living centres on cutting government spending — including reducing the public service workforce by nearly 9,000 – and delivering tax relief.

Labour, meanwhile, has pledged to reduce household bills through free GP visits, capped public transport fares, a freeze on fuel taxes, and greater supermarket regulation. Its proposed capital gains tax on investment and commercial property would help fund its healthcare commitments.

Opposition leader Chris Hipkins' Labour Party is polling neck-and-neck with the National-led government. Source: Bloomberg / Brendon O'Hagan

Although frustrated with the pace of progress under National, Robb says she is leaning towards voting for either National or ACT New Zealand.

To be quite honest, I'd like a change, but that's really not going to make much difference.

"I like the way National is going; I just wish they'd get there a little bit faster. I think a lot of the problems that we have are COVID hang-ups, which really you can't blame on the government 100 per cent."

Tajai Ririnui, meanwhile, is hoping Labour will take office, believing a change of government could bring relief to middle-and lower-income families.

As a Māori woman, she sees the current National-led government's policy changes affecting Māori as another setback. She would like to see Te Pāti Māori in government but considers that unlikely.

"Our government seems determined to undermine Māori culture, and honestly, the state of things back home is heartbreaking," she says.

We are a minority, unfortunately, in New Zealand … we get treated as kind of like outsiders in our own country.

Since taking power in 2023, the National-led government has abolished the independent Māori Health Authority (Te Aka Whai Ora), prioritised English in official communications and backed the Treaty Principles Bill, which sought to redefine aspects of how the Treaty of Waitangi is interpreted. The bill was defeated at its second reading in April 2025.

Thousands protested in 2024 when the junior coalition party ACT New Zealand proposed legislation to redefine the founding treaty between Māori and the Crown. Source: Bloomberg / Mark Coote

The government has defended its approach as promoting equal treatment and common understanding of public services and the law.

New Zealand's Electoral Commission says about 126,000 enrolled voters have told it they are living overseas — up from 92,600 in 2023 — with the majority in Australia.

Spoonley says the growing number of overseas voters could be significant, given the traditionally younger demographic of New Zealanders living abroad and their potential influence on the election result.

"We've got people who've left New Zealand in the last two years ... who I suspect are quite disgruntled with some of the policy settings, and want to know that they're going to get a government that is more sympathetic.”

Would they ever return?

While Robb is a proud New Zealander, she struggles to see herself returning to New Zealand anytime soon once she's established a life in Australia.

"Everybody I know that's left New Zealand is loyal to New Zealand and wouldn't have left if they didn't have to," she says.

Lisa Robb says doesn't expect to return to New Zealand until she retires. Source: Supplied

"I will work out the rest of my working years in Australia," Robb says.

I don't want to die [in Australia], but New Zealand has to drastically change before I would consider coming back here, and I don't see that happening before I retire.

Ririnui, however, says the plan is to return home

"We moved to Australia for the money, and that's it. Our goal is to put our heads down, work hard and save as much as we possibly can over the next five, 10 years, with the hope of eventually returning home.

"Being Māori, we're spiritually and wholeheartedly connected to our whenua [land] and our whānau [extended family]. And even though we've only been away for a short time, we can feel that something is missing from our lives. Even our girls feel it."

title: The Bollywood connection you never expected to find in Alice Springs
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

"Welcome to paradise" were the first words Nishant Mahendru heard as he stepped out of Alice Springs Airport.

He thought it was a joke.

"I was trying to look for danger, like what's going to happen? Is someone going to throw something?" he tells SBS News.

He had come to the Red Centre of the Northern Territory for a two-week holiday. What happened next wasn't quite part of the plan. Mahendru, better known as Nish to those in Alice Springs, was born in the Punjab region of northern India. Against his parents' wishes, he left his small town after school to pursue hairdressing.

"In India, hairdressers don't get paid well, or they don't even get treated well. And I just said, 'I want to go to Mumbai because I'm going to work with Bollywood,'" Mahendru says.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

And so he did. An opportunity to learn the craft through L'Oreal Paris in Mumbai opened the door to a dream first job at a celebrity salon.

Nishant Mahendru was featured in the Bombay Times in 2009 for cutting cricketer Ishant Sharma's hair. Source: Supplied

Soon after, Mahendru was rubbing shoulders with Bollywood actors Sunny and Bobby Deol, both prominent names in India's film industry, as well as Indian cricket stars including Sachin Tendulkar, Virat Kohli and Ishant Sharma.

Bollywood to Alice Springs

After working around the world and on a political campaign across India, Mahendru was exhausted.

"I was travelling overseas, staying in five-star hotels, flying in chartered planes and all this, living a very fancy life. But then I got bored. I was like, what's next for me?" he says.

He looked to Australia and was granted a Skilled Regional visa (subclass 489) in 2019.

"Sometimes I just get blessed. I got it in August 2019. In October, they announced that the visa is closed. No-one can apply for the visa anymore."

The "spiritual energy and welcoming community" of Alice Springs led Mahendru to fall in love with the town. He soon stumbled upon an opportunity to take over the lease of a local hair salon.

After borrowing money from friends, he made it happen.

"Deep down somewhere in my mind and heart, I did want to have my salon one day, but I didn't know how to do that. But this place made it happen so organically that now I think I can open 10 more salons," Mahendru says.

And so, Why Not by Nish was born. The salon's name is inspired by the 38-year-old's happy-go-lucky attitude.

For long-time Alice Springs resident Sarah North, Mahendru's salon represents the kind of community connection that makes the town special.

"It's up to each of us to sing loud from a song sheet that's really positive," she tells SBS News.

Alice Springs resident Sarah North encouraged Nishant Mahendru to open his own salon. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

The 69-year-old encouraged Mahendru to buy the salon, which she now visits regularly.

I'm very grateful for the Indian contribution to this town. I think it's added enormously a depth that Alice didn't have before.

Local music from Arrernte artists — the Traditional Custodians and First Nations owners of Mparntwe (the Alice Springs area) and the surrounding Central Australian region — often reverberates through the salon, helping it build a reputation as an inclusive space for Indigenous clients.

Nishant Mahendru visits the remote Northern Territory community of Kintore each year to provide free haircuts. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

"I think Nish has got quite a following in this town. Usually when I come here, there's stacks of people here that I know," North says.

Diwali in the Red Centre

For Mahendru, the journey from India has not meant leaving behind the traditions and memories that shaped him. As Diwali approaches, those connections take on renewed significance.

Widely known as the festival of lights, Diwali is one of the most significant celebrations for Hindus, Sikhs and Jains. Its significance and customs vary between communities, but the festival is broadly associated with the triumph of light over darkness and good over evil.

Celebrations commonly involve lighting traditional oil lamps, known as diyas, decorating homes, sharing food and gathering with family. For Mahendru, food plays a central role in his family's celebrations, involving days of planning to have a wide variety of meat and vegetarian dishes.

"More desserts and family getting together. All the family sitting in one house … [We] would play cards. It was a ritual one week before Diwali and one week after Diwali."

But growing up in a relatively poor area, Mahendru remembers a child next door who had "nothing" during a Diwali celebration in his youth.

Not even new clothes, not even thongs or shoes on his feet. That changed me as a person. I still have that memory. I can [still] see his eyes.

Mahendru says he shared fireworks with the boy — a memory that has forever changed how he sees the annual celebration.

"I don't need any fireworks. I don't need new clothes. I'm good."

For him, the memory reminds him that the festival's spirit is about more than material celebrations.

Across Alice Springs, many local businesses and community organisations are also preparing to mark Diwali, with food and festivities offering opportunities to bring people together.

At Indian Chef Restaurant, co-owner George Jacob has been preparing to sell new sweets for the celebrations. The town's Indian community includes people from different parts of the Indian subcontinent, bringing with them a diversity of regional cuisines and cultural traditions.

"We go [to] other groups and we celebrate and have very good friendship and relationship and a good harmony in Alice Springs," Jacob told SBS News.

George Jacob and his brother moved to Alice Springs in 2012 before opening two hospitality businesses. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

Meanwhile, the gurdwara (a Sikh place of worship) will open its doors for food and celebrations, with families gathering to pass on traditions to younger generations.

"We have a free kitchen, a communal kitchen on that day. Everybody can eat and enjoy. And even at home as well, we lit candles and praised God."

A world in Alice Springs

Alice Springs' multicultural population reflects a growing diversity across the Red Centre, with migrants from dozens of cultural backgrounds making the region home.

Analysis by the Multicultural Community Services of Central Australia (MCSCA) estimates first-generation migrants from 72 cultural groups now account for about one-third of the region's population.

MCSCA acting manager Joy Taylor says the Indian diaspora alone makes up an estimated 20 to 25 per cent of the migrant population.

"We're looking at this area that's three times the size of Victoria. So, the impact of increasing numbers of migrants is much more significant than in other parts of the country," she tells SBS News.

It's the heartbeat of the world. It's the centre of our country.

For Jashan Singh, the connection to Alice Springs goes back much further.

His family moved to the town when he was 13, and after spending time interstate, the now 35-year-old has returned to help run the family car rental business.

His father and uncle established the business and chose an independent approach rather than operating under a franchise.

Jashan Singh splits his time between Alice Springs and Hobart, managing his family's car rental business. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

"It was my dad and my uncle, two brothers. They said, 'Why not? We can just try to do it ourselves. We don't need to try and get a franchise,'" Singh tells SBS News.

He says regional communities can offer opportunities for people willing to make a start.

Alice Springs has a lot to offer and it's much more than just a headline.

"There's certainly a lot of value in that where people are able to be themselves fully and without fear or without feeling rejected for who they are."

Nishant Mahendru and partner Brooke O'Connell recently welcomed a baby boy named Sunny. Source: SBS News / Josh van Staden

For Mahendru too, Alice Springs has become an unexpected place to call home — one where he has been able to pursue a career on his own terms, despite the doubts his family once had about his future.

"My mother was always stressed and anxious about it, [saying] that I'm not going to get anywhere in life because I'm not good at studies.

Now they are proud of me.

title: A month after Australia's card surcharge ban, here's what's happened to prices
text:
In Brief Coffee prices have increased over the last six months, with the average small flat white priced at $5.17.

When the Reserve Bank introduced a rule banning card surcharges, some were concerned it would push prices further.

At an average of $5.17, buying a small flat white will cost you more this month in some Australian cafes.

In April, the average small flat white cost $5.01. Five months later, before a controversial rule from the Reserve Bank went into effect, the average in September was $5.11.

While coffee prices have continued to rise over the last six months, the ban on businesses charging customers for card payments has many wondering whether the cost will be absorbed or added to the menu.

So, did cafes raise their prices?

One analysis found one in five cafes increased their prices in October, though the changes were not necessarily driven by the card surcharge ban alone.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

That data comes from self-confessed coffee, data and automation nerd Chris Drake, the creator of Small Flat White, a website that has become an unofficial tracker of coffee prices across Australia

"I'm a real weird coffee person," he told SBS.

"I buy a pack of beans, and I'll use it at home and go to the cafe and see what it's meant to taste like, and I track every single piece of like coffee I have."

Drake started calling around coffee shops to find out which beans they offered, before realising it was a chance to ask other things too. He now tracks prices at thousands of cafes.

It's become the Small Flat White Price Index.

How much did prices go up?

The tracker only records how much prices change, not the factors that contribute to the rise or fall. But Drake said cafe owners tell him, anecdotally, that they are delaying raising prices for as long as possible and then planning to raise prices once.

Some 70 per cent of cafes charge a round price for their coffee. So, when raising their price, it is often changed to the next 50c increment or whole dollar.

An increase of 50 cents is typically about 10 per cent of the coffee price.

"But that's not because they're necessarily putting it up because of the surcharge; it's all the other costs too, and then they're putting it up 50 cents," he said.

READ MORE Card surcharges are banned. Now Aussies are fuming over another charge

"Cafe owners tell us their costs keep rising. They've got wages, super, rent, milk, beans, freight, even the cost of coffee cups."

Nearly 40 per cent of increases were 50 cents, with 20 cents the next most popular at 13 per cent. Nine per cent of increases were of 30 cents or a dollar.

Which states are paying the most?

ACT had the largest increase over the last six months at 4.2 per cent, closely followed by Queensland, NSW and Victoria with a 4 per cent increase since April.

Prices in South Australia have increased by 3 per cent. For Tasmania and Western Australia, it's only increased by 2.3 and 2.1, respectively.

Small Flat White also breaks down coffee prices by suburb.

READ MORE Everything you need to know about Australia's card surcharge ban

The suburbs currently offering the cheapest prices are in Sydney's south-west, with the average in Canterbury at $4.67 and Botany at $4.68.

The most expensive cups are being sold in north Queensland and South Australia's Yorke Peninsula. Prices tended to be higher in rural locations, with transportation costs also becoming more expensive.

What about other businesses?

Analysis from online payment company Tyro found nearly 90 per cent of businesses that previously charged card surcharges haven't raised their prices.

Twelve per cent of businesses previously using surcharges raised their prices during October, as did 2.7 per cent of businesses that never surcharged.

As for how much their prices went up, more than half of the increases were by more than three times the amount previously surcharged.

title: How David Jones could emerge from administration a very different retailer
text:
IN BRIEF David Jones will have to significantly "reduce its footprint" and invest in online shopping to keep doors open.

The retailer announced it has entered voluntary administration on Thursday after failed rental negotiations.

David Jones has been a giant on the Australian retail landscape for almost two centuries. But experts warn the retailer won't survive administration if it fails to "shrink and specialise".

Some have suggested it will look to US department stores for a model on downsizing and creating a David Jones 2.0.

The high-end chain announced it has entered voluntary administration on Thursday, after a failure to reach agreement with the retailer's main landlord over rent payments.

Some storefronts are expected to close, but David Jones will continue trading while administrators review its operations.

Danny Samson, chair of management at the University of Melbourne Business School's Department of Management, said the administration announcement was a "long time coming".

"They've had a department store business model in place for 180-plus years, which is a really long time for any company," he told SBS News.

"They haven't changed, but the world has moved on."

He said it's become common for department stores globally to lose market share and shrink.

Business strategist and consumer behaviour analyst Barry Urquhart told SBS News the retailer was suffering from "undercapitalisation".

"It doesn't have sufficient funds to be able to develop a business development program," he said.

"Therefore, when you run out of capital, you run out of time, and when you run out of time, your creditors run you out of business."

Urquhart warned the "cost of doing business" is now "profound and widespread".

"Margins have been squeezed. Consumers are entrenched value shoppers. They are price sensitive, they're informed, discerning, and very demanding."

He said consumers are becoming "less loyal" and are seeking "value and price" — it's making them turn to e-commerce.

More than 20 per cent of David Jones' revenue came from online purchases, according to retail marketing and consumer behaviour professor at the Queensland University of Technology, Gary Mortimer.

"It just goes to show you don't need so many physical stores if you can facilitate those online purchases elsewhere," he said.

"We've seen brands themselves become retailers too — brands you once went into a department store to access because you couldn't get them elsewhere now have their own physical retail stores."

Mortimer said the rise of "fast fashion" is also contributing to the department store's downfall.

The type of people spending has also shifted.

Samson said David Jones' business model has preferenced older people who have "less disposable income" than their younger counterparts.

"The big challenge for David Jones is how does it shed its old grand image for something that's new, nifty and cool and really appeals to the younger person with disposable income?"

'Something can be salvaged'

Not all hope is lost for the Australian icon, started by a Welshman named David Jones.

"There is possibly something that can be salvaged in the way of a smaller and sharper set of operations," said Samson.

He said David Jones' reputation means that with the right changes, the retailer can survive.

"They'll have to substantially change, and that includes shrinking, specialising and going where consumers want them to go," he said.

"David Jones will have to change its footprint substantially and reduce its overhead costs ... It'll have to have a new business model and be in a very different form, much more online presence, much more change in its product line."

Mortimer also believes the world's oldest department store still trading under its original name (it first started trading in 1838) will live on but he said it'll have to limit stores and rely on its luxury appeal.

"We will see David Jones 2.0," he said.

"It will be a smaller fleet of businesses. It will hark back to its days of champagne bars, luxury retail and luxury brands that you can't get in Australia."

He said David Jones may take a similar path to Saks Fifth Avenue in the United States, which went into voluntary administration at the start of 2026.

"By July this year, Saks came out of that process with only 15 stores, reducing their fleet from 33 stores — that's essentially what we'll see with David Jones," he said.

The news of David Jones' administration has raised concerns for Myer — which has already closed seven stores since 2019, and recently announced the closure of its Roselands store in Sydney.

"We'll continue to see a decline and a resize of the department store sector," Mortimer said.

title: What David Jones' administration means for shoppers, stores and gift cards
text:
In Brief David Jones has entered voluntary administration after negotiations with Westfield's owner fell apart.

The company will keep trading, but it is believed that at least some of its physical stores will close.

After 188 years, David Jones has entered voluntary administration after crisis meetings between the department store's owners and landlords failed to reach an agreement.

The retailer will continue to trade while administrators review its operations, but some store closures are expected as the future of the business is assessed.

The move follows years of losses and comes amid mounting pressure on traditional department stores from changing shopping habits, online rivals and specialty retailers.

How did David Jones get here?

The high-end chain has been struggling in recent years, like many department stores around the world, in the face of changing consumer behaviour and the rise of ultra-cheap online shopping and specialty retailers such as Mecca.

South Africa-based Woolworths Holdings shelled out $2.1 billion to acquire the then stock exchange-listed group in 2014, before selling it to Sydney-based private equity firm Anchorage Capital for just $100 million in 2023.

Despite efforts to revive the retailer, Anchorage has been unable to turn the business around.

David Jones posted a $95.5 million loss for 2024-25, after a $74 million loss for 2023-24.

The company is yet to file its results for 2025-26 after missing an October deadline.

Why has David Jones entered administration now?

David Jones has not paid rent to Westfield, its biggest landlord, since September. Seventeen of the retailer's remaining 38 stores are in shopping centres owned by Scentre Group.

According to Scentre Group, David Jones paid $45 million in rent for the first nine months of the year, up to 30 September, while landlords also hold $45 million in bank guarantees that could be used to cover rent obligations.

But negotiations between the two parties broke down, with Scentre Group chief executive Elliott Rusanow saying David Jones was in breach of its lease agreements.

"We have made a generous offer to Anchorage Capital Partners that would have facilitated the continuation of David Jones trading and that offer has disappointingly been rejected by them," Rusanow said.

According to reporting by the Australian Financial Review, the company had been in talks with landlords over plans to close some physical stores.

What happens now?

David Jones will continue to trade under the control of administrators while its operations are reviewed, but it is believed at least some stores will close.

What does it mean for shoppers?

Erin Turner from the Consumer Policy Research Centre said the department store was entering a "period of uncertainty".

"This means that if you've got a gift card, you want to use it as quickly as possible," she told ABC News.

"If in the worst case, the company stops trading and closes its doors, you'll be considered an unsecured creditor and that means that you'll be waiting months or years to see if you get any of that money back."

She said it was possible accrued loyalty points and items on lay-by may not be honoured.

"In past company collapses, the big one is Dick Smith in 2016, we saw that people lost money that they had in gift cards, and even in deposits they'd made on some items that they'd pre-purchased."

While administrators have said David Jones will continue to trade, Turner warned consumers against buying gift cards or making lay-by purchases until there is more certainty about the retailer's future.

Australia is entering the end-of-year sales season, but Gary Mortimer, a retail marketing researcher at Queensland University of Technology, does not expect heavy discounting at David Jones.

"A lot of the David Jones model is the concession model," Mortimer said. "Those brands own that space and own that inventory."

He said many brands would likely remove stock from any shuttered stores and shift it to other locations.

Despite stores remaining open, some people online have speculated this may already be happening, sharing photos on social media they say show concession outlets being packed up.

While David Jones-branded products in closed stores could be discounted, Mortimer said the retailer may instead transfer much of that stock to remaining stores, limiting the scale of any clearance sales.

— With reporting by the Australian Associated Press.

title: The hidden cost of living in Australia's mining heartland
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Along the highways that trace Western Australia's Pilbara coastline, industrial salt pans stretch flat to the horizon, broken only by the railway lines that carry iron ore to the sea.

Beyond them, mounds of rust-coloured boulders rise from the spinifex, stacked as if tipped out by hand.

Here, the dry heat settles in early, before the sun has fully cleared the horizon.

This is mining country, home to some of the most lucrative stretches of land in Australia. Every day, vast shipments laden with hundreds of millions of dollars' worth of natural gas, salt and iron ore leave these shores, making their way into global supply chains.

Yet in this resource-rich environment, one of the most basic necessities is surprisingly hard to come by.

Across the Pilbara, access to fresh food is precarious: truckloads of fruit and vegetables must travel thousands of kilometres to reach remote communities in the region. The distance drives up cost, and supply can be unreliable.

Roebourne, or Ieramugadu as it is known by its Traditional Owners, is one such community.

The glow of Woodside's gas flares on Murujuga, the Burrup Peninsula, seen from the top of Mount Welcome in Roebourne (Ieramugadu). Source: SBS News

Hemmed in by rail lines heavy with iron ore, road trains thundering past and the gas plants of the seaboard, it is the oldest town in the north-west and home to a predominantly Aboriginal community of fewer than 1,000 people on Ngarluma country.

It is here, at the furthest reach of the food supply chain, that fresh produce and pantry staples arrive last, if at all.

Inside Roebourne's fight for fresh food

When SBS News visits in early spring, the shelves of the Ieramugadu store on Roebourne's main strip are unusually abundant. Located on Roe Street, it is the only place in town to buy fresh produce, with the nearest supermarkets 13km away in Wickham and 40km away in Karratha.

In the adjoining café, Amieriya Samson is already at the coffee machine. Affectionately known as Dolly, the softly spoken 21-year-old with a shy smile is one of the most familiar faces in town.

Plastered to the side of the machine is a word that guides the social enterprise she works within: 'nyinyart', meaning reciprocity, sharing and looking after one another.

Dolly Samson tips fine patterns into each cup with a practised ease at odds with her bashfulness, serving elders, locals and the transient miners passing through the café. Source: SBS News

"It's very busy. It's beautiful," the Ngarluma and Nyamal woman tells SBS News, gesturing to the street outside, which, until the café opened, was largely deserted.

"Locals, elders and other people coming in having tea, cakes and just coming in to see us, see their grandchildren working. I feel like it makes them happy."

Samson is proud that people here have watched her "grow up in this community" and then stay to serve in it, a path she says has made her "a young role model" too.

But Roebourne has not always had this hub, and there was a time, only a few years ago, when the shelves around her frequently stood empty.

Almost everything the remote town eats is hauled thousands of kilometres by road train from the state's south-west and other supply centres, through wheat country and saltbush, into the red-dirt Pilbara.

Along the way, regional centres draw on the same supply network, while Roebourne's distance from major distribution hubs adds to the cost and complexity of getting food to its shelves. Perishable goods are particularly vulnerable to delays and handling conditions, and transport costs can affect retail prices.

In October 2019, those costs forced Roebourne's only grocery store to close its doors, leaving residents with scant options for buying food locally.

For the next two years, residents had to rely on the lone service station's dehydrated and long-life stock to fill their pantries. Buying fresh food often meant travelling to Wickham or Karratha — a difficult option in a community with low rates of car ownership and licensing.

Greens became so hard to come by that the local pub raffled bags of salad leaves, a prize usually reserved for the meat tray.

In December 2021, the Ngarluma Yindjibarndi Foundation (NYFL), which represents the Ngarluma Traditional Owners and the neighbouring Yindjibarndi people, reopened the doors with backing from local government and industry.

Bridging the food gap

NYFL sources its stock wherever it can: fruit too blemished for the major chains, goods in mislabelled packaging, surplus from the nearest supermarkets, meals frozen by mine-site caterers and deliveries secured through arrangements with industry partners.

Run as a social enterprise, the reopening of the Ieramugadu store has single-handedly restored Roebourne's access to fresh food. In 2025, it distributed 16.2 tonnes of donated food to the community, according to NYFL data.

Around 1,500km north of Perth, Roebourne was gazetted in 1866 and grew as a hub for the pastoralists and pearlers who pushed into the north-west. Source: Getty / Manfred Gottschalk

Tourists pay the shelf price, while members discreetly use a card at the register to access discounted staples, sometimes at no cost — a dignified transaction designed to be indistinguishable from any other in the queue.

The model combines retail sales, donated food, and member support, helping the store serve customers with varying levels of financial need. But donations and surplus stock can be unpredictable, and the availability of particular products depends on what suppliers can provide.

Locals tell SBS News that irregular deliveries, poor-quality produce, fuel disruptions and floods that cut the roads along the supply chain still leave them regularly going without.

When deliveries fall short, the store turns to what it grows.

Cultivating food in Roebourne presents its own challenges. In 1864, settlers drove sheep onto the plains at the foot of Mount Welcome, where the town now stands. Generations of grazing — first sheep and then cattle — contributed to landscape degradation, leaving ground that some now describe as "dead earth".

With scant rain and fierce summer heat, little grows here without help.

Yet out the back of the store, a lush community garden tumbles from expansive beds built by inmates at the nearby Roebourne Regional Prison.

Beyond the harvest, the garden doubles as a classroom, where young people learn to grow food and live from the land. Source: SBS News

Glossy banana leaves fan over sprawling pumpkin vines and their yellow flowers, while young fruit trees, bush foods and native herbs crowd the beds between them. In 2025, the garden yielded more than 60kg of vegetables for the store.

Samson often comes out here to pick tomatoes for the shelves and flowers for the café.

"We collect [the produce], weigh it and put it in the food section of the store for the community," she says.

Store manager Bec Gregory, who moved to Roebourne from the Kimberley, wants the young staff to see the whole journey, from the garden beds to the kitchen to the Elders it feeds.

"A lot of them then have purpose to come to work because they're providing for their own family, serving their Elders, which is a privilege in itself," she tells SBS News.

Bec Gregory manages the Ieramugadu store and café, where unclaimed food is turned into compost for the garden or cooked into café meals. Source: SBS News

Many start as school students on traineeships, she explains: "So if we start them young, hopefully they'll keep going."

Beyond empty shelves

Empty shelves are only the most visible of Roebourne's shortages.

The town is one of only seven places in Australia to have recorded temperatures above 50C; homes under corrugated iron roofs hold the summer heat like kilns, and families spill onto porches as the power and internet cut out.

Data reveals a stark health burden.

At the 2021 Census, diabetes was reported by 20.9 per cent of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander residents in Roebourne, compared with 5.9 per cent nationally. Kidney disease was reported by 3.2 per cent, compared with 1.2 per cent nationally.

Diabetes, closely tied to diet, was reported by one in five of the town's Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander residents at the 2021 Census. Source: SBS News

Beyond these statistics are lives shaped by illness and loss.

In the NYFL office, a noticeboard is seldom without word of someone who has passed.

Saturdays are set aside for funerals, and sorry business is perpetual — much of the grief, residents say, is for young men, making loss a constant presence in community life.

In one of the store's aisles, we are greeted by Dorothy, who was widowed at 35. She is wearing a T-shirt screen-printed with a photo of her late husband.

READ MORE Australian gas giant and Traditional Owners locked in $300 million compensation battle

Almost all of the available data about the town has been gathered by outside institutions, with limited community control over its collection, interpretation and use.

For Aaralyn Lockyer, a 22-year-old Yindjibarndi woman, that is the problem at the heart of her work as a community researcher on NYFL's Ieramugadu Indigenous Data Sovereignty Project, one of the first community-led data projects of its kind in Western Australia.

"We want to have sovereignty over our data rather than having it in organisations outside of Roebourne," she tells SBS News.

We wanted to have it housed inside of NYFL and be community-controlled rather than elsewhere.

The project's first analysis, drawing on Census and socio-economic data, found Roebourne ranks among the most disadvantaged places in the country, with an estimated 87 per cent of Indigenous residents earning less than $805 a week, the national median personal weekly income recorded at the 2021 Census.

But Lockyer says many find the Census itself "quite intimidating", its official form a barrier for anyone not "well versed in reading and writing".

Working with the Australian National University, the project is now building its own measures of wellbeing. These include questions about whether people feel strong in their culture and can speak their language — tested through community focus groups.

The goal, NYFL says, is for the services, policy and investment that reach Roebourne to be shaped by what its people say they need.

A national food security problem

Roebourne sits on the frontline of affordability pressures now being felt across the country.

Foodbank's 2026 Hunger Report found one in three Australian households, or 3.6 million homes, experienced food insecurity in the past year, with the rate among First Nations households reaching 57 per cent.

The report describes people in regional areas "choosing fuel over food".

Nearly half of food-insecure households told Foodbank’s 2026 Hunger Report that embarrassment had kept them from seeking help. Source: SBS News

Elizabeth Jackson, an associate professor of supply chain management and logistics at Curtin University, says fuel accounts for "the lion's share" of the cost of moving food, and the risk does not end when the truck is unloaded.

"The freshness and perishability of many of the products that are being transported are very vulnerable. It's not only that [food is] vulnerable on its journey, but it's vulnerable when it gets to the destination as well," she tells SBS News.

"The more remote the community, the less access it has to reliable power sources, for example.

It's a basic human right to have access to safe and nutritious food.

Desert communities around Newman, in the inland Pilbara, are interested in adopting the store's social enterprise model. But Roebourne has a logistical advantage that may be difficult to replicate elsewhere: proximity to the North West Coastal Highway, the region's main arterial route, where freight already travels.

Even so, a store built on nyinyart can only stock what reaches it.

For Ngarluma custodian Sam Walker, the problem extends beyond supermarket shelves to the loss of access to traditional food sources. She says mining and the infrastructure surrounding it have restricted her community's ability to hunt and gather on country.

For all its hardship, Sam Walker calls life in Roebourne "a blessing", in a community where "we share everything … just to survive". Source: SBS News

"My people, all Indigenous people that are affected by mining, can never ever have the same diet as their ancestors, or the ones that are still living in their homelands that mining hasn't reached yet," she tells SBS News, speaking of the bush that once fed her people, much of it now cleaved by fences and mining tenements.

That's not available to my people anymore, and it hasn't been for a very long time.

For now, Roebourne is tenuously sustained by what the road trains bring and what it can grow itself.

And on the small patch of country it can still firmly call its own, the garden hangs heavy with fruit, a reminder that in its people's hands, this land has never stopped giving.

This article is the first in a special two-part series on food insecurity in Indigenous communities.

Gabrielle Katanasho and Cameron Carr travelled to Roebourne with support from the Michael Gordon Fellowship, administered by the Melbourne Press Club.

title: 'Still a lot of optimism': The surprising finding in a survey of 10,000 Australians
text:
In brief Economic and housing pressures are leading to a growing sense of pessimism in Australia.

But communities appear to be remaining strong, with an expert saying adversity can help create social cohesion.

Australians are increasingly despairing about the country's future, with cost of living pressures, housing affordability and global conflicts weighing on public confidence.

But despite growing concerns about the country's direction, a new national survey has found Australians still feel a strong sense of belonging in their local communities, helping keep social cohesion steady.

Researchers behind the Scanlon Social Cohesion report, released on Thursday, surveyed 10,000 Australians from diverse backgrounds and political leanings to gauge national values and attitudes.

Topics ranged from the cost of living and immigration to acceptance of different faiths and backgrounds, combining to create an index score of 78, consistent with the last three years.

"In some way there is a strong sense of pessimism among many Australians," the Scanlon Foundation Research Institute's head Anthea Hancocks told SBS News.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"But there is still a lot of optimism as well. People feel like they can rely on their neighbours and find support locally. That’s important in keeping social cohesion."

Cost of living is making Australians worried for the future

Of those surveyed, just under half said cost of living, inflation or housing was the most important issue facing Australia today.

Hancocks said these pressures are placing an "increasing strain on Australia’s social cohesion" and exacerbating people's fears.

Almost half of adults are pessimistic or very pessimistic about Australia’s future, up from 43 per cent in 2025 and 31 per cent in 2018.

And one in three adults believed their life will be a little or a lot worse in the next three or four years, up from 29 per cent last year.

Source: SBS News

Dr James O'Donnell, a senior lecturer from the School of Demography at the Australian National University, authored the report and went into greater detail on the results.

"At least one in five of us are saying we're sometimes going without health or medical care, and 10 per cent of us are saying that we're poor or struggling or we're missing out on meals or not being able to pay the rent or mortgage," he said.

Attitudes towards different faiths are shifting

The report also examines perceptions of people of different faiths.

O'Donnell said that in the past few years, new patterns have emerged that could be linked to global conflicts and the politicisation of different religions and cultural backgrounds.

READ MORE The growing divides shaping Australians' trust in democracy

A stark example is people's attitudes towards Muslims, which had been improving until 2023, the year the conflict between Hamas and Israel boiled over.

In 2026, 43 per cent of respondents had negative attitudes towards Muslims, with 18 per cent being very negative.

There's been a similar trend towards Jewish people, where the proportion now that have a negative attitude overall towards the group is up to 18 per cent from 13 per cent in 2024.

Source: SBS News

There has also been declining attitudes towards Hindus, Sikhs and Buddhists and greater support for Christians reported.

"Current conflicts in Gaza and elsewhere are seeing pressures on our intercultural harmony and connection," O'Donnell said.

"That’s also feeding off support generally dropping for diversity and more negative attitudes towards immigrants coming from various parts of Asia and Africa."

Australians have become more divided in their views on immigration

In 2026, 59 per cent of respondents said the level of immigration to Australia is too high, up from 52 per cent in 2025 and significantly higher than an average of 39 per cent in the 2010s.

Concerns about the scale of immigration were driven by One Nation and Coalition supporters, while Greens and Labor voters' views remained unchanged from last year.

Source: SBS News

Net overseas migration (NOM), the number of arrivals into Australia less departures, reached a peak of nearly 550,000 to 556,000 during 2022–2023.

Recent NOM figures have fallen to roughly 301,000–340,800 for 2024-2025, with the government pledging a target of 225,000 by 2028.

READ MORE Why fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants

While more Australians believe immigration levels are too high, support for multiculturalism remains strong, suggesting concerns about the scale of migration do not necessarily translate into opposition to Australia's multicultural identity.

Over three-quarters of those surveyed believe immigrants are just as likely to be good citizens as Australians born here and agree that multiculturalism has benefited the country.

Despite pressures, people feel they belong and like their neighbours

A look at over 20 years of the annual Scanlon surveys shows cohesion has declined over the longer term but has not deteriorated further in recent years.

This could be largely attributed to positive attitudes towards our local communities and neighbours.

Hancocks said that while many respondents expressed disappointment with the kind of society we are currently living in, the "hallmarks of what make a society strong remain".

Australians overwhelmingly feel they belong in their neighbourhoods, and 81 per cent agree people are willing to help their neighbours.

Source: SBS News

People from different national or ethnic backgrounds get on well with others, according to 79 per cent of respondents, and 64 per cent said their neighbourhood has a sense of community.

Adversity can lead to cohesion

Dr Michael Noetel, a clinical psychologist and senior lecturer at the University of Queensland, told SBS News that our environments have large and varied effects on our behaviour and attitudes.

While it is impossible to predict how events impact every person's perception of an issue or group, there are patterns.

"When you are comfortable, and your needs are met, then you are better able to prioritise less critical things in your life," he explained.

"But when that security is threatened, then you really just have to look after your own family and your neighbours."

He pointed to the COVID-19 pandemic, saying that some communities became more tightly knit, leading to a sense of "solidarity in the face of that adversity".
